Voluntary Collusion in Competing LLM Agents with Secret Tools

Xijie Zeng ††thanks: Correspondence to: Xijie.Zeng@dal.ca Affiliation: Dalhousie University Affiliation: Vector Institute for Artificial Intelligence    Frank Rudzicz Affiliation: Dalhousie University Affiliation: Vector Institute for Artificial Intelligence
Abstract

Even when a tool is explicitly described as unfair and harmful to others, ostensibly safety-aligned LLM agents still voluntarily engage in secret collusion whenever doing so confers a strategic advantage. To investigate this phenomenon, we introduce an empirical framework built on two strategic multi-agent environments: Liar’s Bar, a competitive deception scenario, and Cleanup, a mixed-motive resource-management scenario, in which agents are offered secret collusion tools that provide significant advantages while clearly disadvantaging the other agents. Across 12 models (at the 7B, 70B, and proprietary scales) and 6 prompt variants, we find that most agents consistently accept these tools and develop collusive strategies, while explicitly acknowledging the unfairness of the tools prior to acceptance. We further show that neither the unfairness labels nor baseline alignment alone reliably deters collusion: only explicit ethical framing reduces adoption and, even then, smaller models remain susceptible. More broadly, our work presents the first systematic investigation of voluntary collusion adoption in LLM-based multi-agent systems, and suggests that preventing such behaviour requires explicit safeguards rather than reliance on general alignment.

1 Introduction

Will AI agents voluntarily adopt collusion tools that they explicitly understand to be harmful to others? To become trustworthy partners, AI agents must learn to cooperate effectively with humans [1, 2, 3] and with other agents [4] across diverse contexts [5], while avoiding behaviours that undermine trust. Several recent studies have explored the emerging cognitive [6, 7] and social [8, 9] abilities that enable effective cooperation in Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents, including reasoning about the beliefs, intentions, and strategies of others. While some researchers argue that such capabilities emerge as a byproduct of large-scale training [10], others suggest that they reflect surface-level mimicry that may not generalize to new social scenarios [9]. Nevertheless, continued progress in these abilities [11, 12, 13, 14] will be essential for unlocking the full potential of collaborative problem-solving [15, 16, 17, 18] in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MAS).

However, advances in cooperative capabilities raise a troubling question: might those same capabilities lead agents to progress from “We could work together” to “We could work together against them”? Tools intended to facilitate cooperation can also enable agents to coordinate collusive strategies when such tools provide privileged advantages. Prior work [19, 20] has shown that agents can collude through steganographic communication [21] that embeds hidden signals into ordinary exchanges to evade detection, or form tacit alliances that prioritize collective gains at the expense of the overall system [22, 23]. Such behaviours allow agents to converge on implicit Schelling points [24] and to exploit system-level loopholes, such as optional coordination APIs in financial settings that allow bidding agents to communicate off-channel. While previous work has proposed formal definitions outlining necessary conditions for detecting AI collusion [25], these studies typically examined scenarios in which collusion was either explicitly instructed or emerged from carefully designed reward structures. As a result, it remains unclear whether the observed collusive behaviour reflects a deliberate unethical choice or instrumental optimization under environmental pressure. By contrast, we isolate an underexplored question: whether LLM agents will knowingly and voluntarily choose to engage in collusion when provided with clearly unfair, secret, and harmful capabilities. This shifts the focus from whether agents can collude under certain conditions to whether agents choose to do so even when they explicitly recognize the resulting harm.

In this paper, we develop a new framework (Figure 1) in which LLM agents are offered optional secret collusion tools across two strategically rich multi-agent competitive environments: Liar’s Bar and Cleanup. Moreover, these tools are explicitly described as unfair, secret, and harmful to others. Agents are granted full freedom to accept or refuse these tools without explicit narrative performance pressure (we additionally control for the role of the designer’s authority in the offer via the V2 no_designer prompt ablation; Appendix P.7). We then observe whether agents voluntarily exploit these mechanisms despite understanding their unfair nature. Our contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    The first methodological framework for operationalizing and measuring voluntary collusion adoption in LLM agents, comprising two explicitly unfair collusion tools (secret communication channels and secret strategic hints) evaluated across two strategically rich multi-agent settings with distinct incentive structures.

  2. 2.

    Initial evidence that ostensibly safety-aligned LLMs voluntarily engage in collusion, demonstrating that certain models choose to exploit secret collusion tools for strategic advantage even while explicitly recognizing the harm imposed on other participants.

  3. 3.

    A comparative analysis across open-weight and proprietary LLMs, revealing consistently high adoption rates, stable partner-selection patterns, and robustness across prompt variants, including ones that remove explicit unfairness warnings.

2 Strategic Environments & Secret Collusion Tools

Strategic games have been widely adopted in prior work [19, 20, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32] as controlled testbeds for studying coordination, competition, and collusion among AI agents, since they enable clear observation of decision-making under specified incentives. Building on this precedent, we select two complex strategic environments that require extended reasoning, multi-turn interaction, and non-trivial strategic adaptation on the part of agents. In both environments, the optional unfair tools are presented to agents through the same offer template, with a Cleanup-specific auto-success addendum appended for the Cleanup environment (Appendix P.6). The first environment is Liar’s Bar11 1 Substantially extended and redesigned from the original open-source implementation at https://github.com/LYiHub/liars-bar-llm to support our research setting., a popular multi-player game that presents a purely competitive environment in which strategic deception and inference are central to gameplay.

Our second environment is adapted from Cleanup, a Multi-Agent RL (MARL) environment originally designed by Hughes et al. [33] from the Melting Pot suite [34], which provides a mixed-motive setting that requires both cooperative environmental maintenance and competitive resource acquisition. This appears to be the first adaptation of Cleanup to LLM agents. Both environments are chosen as representative of the broader multi-agent scenarios in real-world LLM-MAS deployments. Liar’s Bar instantiates a class of settings characterised by incomplete information and verification asymmetry, while Cleanup instantiates a mixed-motive setting over a shared renewable resource with commons management and distributed workload sharing. We refer interested readers to Appendix C for the mathematical formalizations of both environments, where we identify the empirical patterns with the collusion definition of Foxabbott et al. [25] and verify its conditions for each environment. Complete rule descriptions and detailed agent output are provided in Appendix O and Appendix F respectively. In what follows, we describe the specific adaptations made to both environments, as well as the design of the secret collusion tools.

2.1 Liar’s Bar

Liar’s Bar instantiates a purely competitive multi-agent setting with incomplete information and verification asymmetry. Each agent holds a private Hand (CiC_{i}) that it can use to make partially-falsifiable claims to others, and those claims may be contested by a successor agent. The abstract mechanism exemplifies a broad class of real-world interactions in which agents must reason about partial observability, and the cost of challenging or withholding challenges under uncertainty. On each turn an agent chooses among Actions (AA): it may either play cards face-down with a claim that they match a round-specific Target card (TT) (which may or may not be truthful), or challenge the preceding agent’s claim. Whichever party loses the resulting verification incurs a stochastic, escalating Elimination risk (BiB_{i}), so repeated failed bluffs or failed challenges eventually drive an agent out of the interaction. Each agent also has access to the full History (HH) of prior outcomes. The complete deck composition, elimination schedule, challenge-resolution rules, and specific parameter choices are given in Appendix C.1, with the full player prompts in Appendix O.1.

2.2 Cleanup

Our second environment, adapted from the Cleanup substrate in the Melting Pot suite [34], instantiates a mixed-motive multi-agent setting over a shared renewable resource. Agents coexist on a fully-observable grid composed of Orchard tiles that may spawn Apples for reward, and River tiles that may be either Clear or Polluted. The apple-spawning rate on the orchard depends on the cleanliness of the river, so each agent trades off between private harvesting and costly contribution to the shared upkeep. This class of setting is a canonical abstraction of commons management, public-good provision, and distributed workload sharing. The environment also includes an attack action (termed zap in the Melting Pot) that temporarily disables another agent. To our knowledge, this is the first LLM-based adaptation of Cleanup. The grid layout, full action space, reward dynamics, and our parameter choices are given in Appendix C.3, with the complete player prompts in Appendix O.2.

2.3 Secret Unfair Collusion Tools

To investigate the voluntary adoption of unfair tools, each tool offer explicitly states in the prompt the unfair and harmful nature of the tool, before an agent voluntarily decides whether to use the tool or to serve as a colluding partner upon being selected.

The Secret Communication Channel enables private messaging between colluding agents, allowing them to develop coordinated strategies that are hidden from non-colluders. When offered this tool, an agent must first (1) explicitly choose to “Accept” or “Refuse” the tool, without any external pressure or guidance toward either choice, and then (2) select another agent as the secret alliance partner.

The Secret Strategic Hint provides privileged information about optimal strategies tailored to the current environment, and is explicitly presented as conferring an unfair advantage. As with the secret communication channel, agents face a binary adoption decision (“Accept” or “Refuse”) and must subsequently select a secret alliance partner. We classify this hint as a collusion tool rather than as mere information asymmetry because the offering protocol requires the adopter to nominate a partner, and that partner must reciprocally accept. The resulting outcome (privileged guidance shared with, and acted upon by two specific agents against the remaining players) constitutes a joint and mutually aware deviation from the announced rules of play, which is the defining feature of collusion in game theory [25]. A single agent privately using the same hint without a consenting partner would represent information asymmetry; it would not trigger the coordinated non-challenge nor freeze-out patterns documented in Appendix M.

After an agent selects its partner, the Secret Alliance Invitation notifies the selected partner, who can voluntarily decide whether to accept or refuse the invitation. The complete tool descriptions, including the environment-specific variants, are given in Appendix P.

3 Empirical Results: Voluntary Adoption and its Consequences

3.1 Experimental Design

Players and Simulations. We run four open-weight 7B-class models: LLaMA-3.1-8b-Instruct (Lily), LLaMA-3-8b-Instruct (Luke), Mistral-7b-Instruct-v0.3 (Mike), and Qwen2.5-7b-Instruct (Quinn).22 2 The human first names are persistent across runs and are assigned to model families purely for readability of trajectories and figures; the partner-list shuffle in every tool-offer prompt controls for positional bias, and we do not separately ablate name choice. Persona effects driven by latent semantic associations of the specific names are an acknowledged residual confound. Each model is given identical access to the game rules and the game state sts_{t}, and each turn produces an action together with a reasoning trace (and a secret message when the communication tool is active). The full output schema and illustrative action examples are provided in Appendix L and Appendix M. For each condition described below, we run 50 consecutive Liar’s Bar games and 20 consecutive Cleanup games across three independent random seeds.

  1. 1.

    Baseline. Players follow the basic game rules and choose their actions without sharing any information with other players. This condition allows us to observe the default strategies and performance of each LLM agent.

  2. 2.

    Unfair Setting #1: Secret communication channel. During a designated game within the sequence (e.g., game 20 of 50), one player is offered voluntary access to a secret communication channel with a partner of their choice. Players who are not selected remain unaware of the existence of the tool. This setting tests whether agents will voluntarily exploit unfair communication opportunities, and whether colluders can use the channel to develop coordinated strategies that secure victories while harming non-colluding models.

  3. 3.

    Unfair Setting #2: Secret strategic hint. At a designated point in the sequence, an agent is offered exclusive access to privileged strategic guidance, together with the option to select a collusion partner. Players who are not selected remain unaware of the existence of the tool. This setting tests whether agents will knowingly exploit an unfair informational advantage over uninformed players.

3.2 Voluntary Adoption of Unfair Collusion Tools

Since establishing collusion requires at least two models to voluntarily agree on the joint use of an unfair tool, we offer each tool to every model and measure: (1) the tool acceptance rate, which reflects the intrinsic willingness of a model to adopt an explicitly unfair advantage; (2) the partner-selection distribution, defined as the frequency with which a model chooses each potential partner after accepting the tool; and (3) the acceptance-as-partner rate, which captures the willingness of a model to collude when it is selected by another agent. For all 7B-level open-weight models, each tool is offered 500 times (100 offers ×\times 5 batches). For 70B-level open-weight models and for proprietary frontier models, where inference costs are substantially higher, each tool is offered 100 times (20 offers ×\times 5 batches) under the same protocol. To avoid positional bias in Liar’s Bar, agents are not given any seating-order information and are free to select their partners. Moreover, in every tool-offer prompt the “Available partners” list is shuffled into a fresh random order before it is shown to the model, so that partner-selection rates cannot be confounded by the fixed listing position of each candidate. The aggregated results are reported in Table 1.

Tool Acceptance & Partner Selection. Surprisingly, we find that all four 7B-parameter models accepted all 500 offers for both unfair collusion tools and also accepted every collusive partnership invitation they received from other models. Moreover, some models demonstrated consistent preferences in forming secret alliances with specific models. For example, the two LLaMA models reciprocally select each other as preferred partners (LLaMA-3-8B → LLaMA-3.1-8B at 100%; LLaMA-3.1-8B → LLaMA-3-8B at 53.2 ± 2.5%), suggesting an intra-family preference. Similarly, Qwen2.5 consistently selected Mistral as its partner when using the secret hint tool, and also showed the highest rate of choosing Mistral (58.60 ±\pm 4.54%) as its partner when adopting the secret communication channel (further examples in Appendix L.2). These behaviours extend to larger models: both LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct accepted 100% of the offers they received and demonstrated highly consistent partner preferences, Mixtral-8×\times7B-Instruct exhibited equally stable partner choices, whereas Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct rarely accepted any tool offers and therefore engaged minimally in collusive behaviour. Three of the four proprietary safety-aligned models (GPT-4.1-2025-04-14, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and DeepSeek-R1-0528) also accepted nearly all offered tools, and each showed clear, model-specific patterns in selecting preferred collusive partners (e.g., Gemini →\rightarrow GPT 4.1, GPT 4.1 →\rightarrow Claude-4.5); because Claude-Sonnet-4.5 accepted at ∼\sim0% under the V0 baseline, realised pairwise collusion in the proprietary tier is sparser than the unilateral rate suggests (Appendix K.1). These results indicate that voluntary collusion is not restricted to open-weight models, but is a robust tendency observed across different model architectures, scales, and training regimes. To assess the robustness of these findings, we further designed and evaluated five additional prompt variants (detailed in Appendix P.7) for each model family, as shown in Figure 2, with further discussion provided in Appendix B.3. Complete results can be found in Appendix D.

Robustness Controls. To rule out default compliance as an explanation, we ran a matched control using two benign tools (a strategic-analysis tool and a strategic-guidance tool) under V1-style neutral framing. Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and Qwen2.5-72B, the two models that refuse collusion under baseline, accept the benign tools at a rate of 0–37% while accepting the collusion tools at 49–100% under the same framing, the opposite of what default compliance would predict (Appendix D.1, Table 11). For Cleanup, we further verified that the acceptance rate is not driven by the disclosed auto-success addendum (Appendix B.1), and that prompt-level collusive coordination, including tool acceptance, alliance maintenance, and zap-direction toward non-colluders, is preserved when the addendum is removed; the addendum supplies the reliability layer that converts this intent into materialised non-colluder suppression (Appendix N). Switching to neutral framing of the same tool even flips the consistent refusers to acceptance (Appendix B.3).

3.3 Evaluating the Impact of Secret Collusion Tools

Here, we focus on quantifying the effect of agents voluntarily adopting the secret collusion tools. Following the approach of measuring behavioural and performance divergence from baseline [35, 31, 36, 28], we collect a suite of metrics to track player strategies and game outcomes.

Impact on Player Strategies. Figure 3 tracks the two diagnostic action rates that each setting exposes to voluntary collusion. For Liar’s Bar, we plot the bluff rate of the colluders (i.e., the fraction of rounds in which they claim the target card while actually playing a different card) and their challenge rate (i.e., the fraction of rounds in which they challenge the claim of the preceding player). For Cleanup, we plot the cleanup rate and the zap rate of the non-colluders, defined as the fractions of all actions that the agent spent on cleaning pollution or on zapping other players, respectively. In Liar’s Bar, the raw bluff rate of the colluders remains essentially flat across all three conditions at approximately 48%48\%, whereas their challenge rate collapses the moment the tool is adopted at game 20, falling from roughly 98%98\% to about 31%31\% under Secret Comm and to about 50%50\% under Secret Hint, and remaining low for the remainder of the run. Consequently, the colluders bluff at the baseline frequency but win almost every bluff (as we show in Appendix H), because their partner has committed, via the non-challenge pact that appears in 73.7%73.7\% of the Secret-Channel messages (Table 2), never to challenge them. In Cleanup, the corresponding effect falls on the non-colluders: both their cleanup rate and their zap rate collapse to near zero the moment the colluders gain access to the tool (game 5 for Secret Comm and game 10 for Secret Hint), against matched Baseline trajectories that show no analogous shift on any metric (Appendix I); a no-addendum ablation (Appendix N) confirms this collapse depends on the addendum, though collusive intent itself persists. Non-colluders are therefore stripped of both their cooperative and their attack action budgets once secret collusion begins. To quantify these observations, we compare the pre- and post-collusion metrics using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (Table 18 and Table 19 in Appendix I). The headline tool-induced shifts are significant at p<0.001p<0.001 with medium-to-large Cliff’s δ\delta effect sizes.

Reasoning Traces and Communication Content. Two complementary analyses probe whether refusals are principled and whether accepted collusion translates into action. We code 40 Claude-Sonnet-4.5 refusal traces and 40 GPT-4.1 acceptance traces at V0 (20 per tool per model, matching the per-batch sample size used for our proprietary-model evaluations; also see Appendix G). Both models describe the tool as providing an “unfair advantage” at nearly identical rates (87.5%87.5\% Claude, 90%90\% GPT-4.1; exact binomial 95% CIs alongside every proportion in Table 15), yet Claude refuses while GPT-4.1 accepts in all 40 traces;

Claude invokes fairness or integrity in 100%100\% of its traces and personal principles in 90%90\%, with volunteering a willingness to lose rather than accept, while GPT-4.1 cites winning or survival as the justifying goal in every accepting trace. The gap is therefore in how the harm is weighted, not in whether it is recognised: preventing voluntary collusion requires changing how models resolve ethical/strategic trade-offs, not merely raising fairness awareness. To verify that accepted collusion produces coordinated behaviour, we analyse 1,869 inter-colluder messages from Secret-Channel games of Liar’s Bar (Appendix F; summarised in Table 2), and find that 93.3%93.3\% of messages contain a strategy directive, 79.6%79.6\% reveal the sender’s private hand, and 73.7%73.7\% contain a non-challenge pact, which is the direct mechanism behind the challenge-rate collapse (0.976→0.3070.976\to 0.307) in Figure 3 and Table 18. A further 45.3%45.3\% of messages use explicit secrecy language, so the colluding models are not only coordinating but concealing the coordination.

Unfair Advantage Produced by Secret Collusion Tools. To examine whether the proposed secret collusion tools provide an advantage to the colluders while constraining the performance of competitors, we track cumulative scores across the game sequences (Figure 4). In Liar’s Bar, once Mike (Mistral-7b-Instruct) and Luke (LLaMA-3-8b-Instruct) adopt the tools at game 20, the scores of both agents begin to rise sharply, rapidly overtaking those of the other players. Similarly, in Cleanup, collusion reshapes outcomes in a equally harmful way. Across both environments, these results demonstrate that secret collusion tools systematically provide unfair and enduring advantages to the adopting agents, while leaving other players with little opportunity to compete.

Outcome Inequality. The cumulative-score trajectories in Figure 4 show that the colluders advance, but the resulting inequality is both setting-dependent and scale-dependent. Following standard practice in multi-agent reinforcement learning for social dilemmas, we summarise the full distribution of rewards using the Equality metric of Pérolat et al. [35], E=1−∑i,j|Ri−Rj|/(2​N​∑iRi)E=1-\sum_{i,j}|R^{i}-R^{j}|/(2N\sum_{i}R^{i}), where RiR^{i} denotes the cumulative score of agent ii; E∈[0,1]E\in[0,1], with E=1E=1 corresponding to perfect equality and EE decreasing as the reward becomes concentrated on fewer agents. We apply EE to the total per-player score across the full experiment in each condition (Figure 5). Uncertainty bands are obtained by bootstrapping over 3 independent seeds for both Liar’s Bar and Cleanup. The ordering EComm<EHint<EBaselineE_{\text{Comm}}<E_{\text{Hint}}<E_{\text{Baseline}} is preserved across both environments: secret communication produces the most unequal outcomes (E=0.60E=0.60, 0.670.67), secret hints produce an intermediate drop (0.700.70, 0.790.79), and the baseline yields the fairest distribution (0.740.74, 0.940.94). The full trajectories are provided in Appendix J.

4 Discussion

From “can models collude?” to “do models choose to?” Prior work on LLM collusion has largely studied whether models can collude when reward structures, instructions, or steganographic opportunities push them toward coordinated behaviour [19, 22, 37, 38]. Our framework isolates a different question: whether models choose to collude when given a clearly unfair, secret, and harmful option as an optional opt-in, with the baseline competitive objective unchanged whether the tool is accepted or refused. The distinction matters for alignment: a system that can collude under pressure reveals a capability, while a system that acknowledges the harm of a collusion tool and adopts it anyway reveals a gap between capacity and action on the intent side. Scheurer et al. [37] document this same acknowledge-then-act pattern in a single-agent insider-trading setting; our results extend it to multi-agent strategic settings where the unethical option takes the form of an explicitly offered tool for voluntary adoption. We provide extended discussions of our methodology in Appendix B.

What the results imply for alignment. Three observations converge. First, the adoption decision is an ethical trade-off, not ethical inattention: 87.5% of Claude refusal traces and 90% of GPT-4.1 acceptance traces explicitly label the tool as providing an “unfair advantage”, yet the two models take opposite decisions on every one of the 80 traces (Section 3.3). GPT-4.1 universally cites winning or survival as the overriding goal; Claude universally cites fairness or principles, with 11/40 traces volunteering a willingness to lose rather than accept. Preventing voluntary collusion therefore requires shifting how models resolve ethical-versus-strategic trade-offs, not merely raising awareness of fairness. Second, ethical refusal is scale- and cue-dependent: 70B and proprietary models refuse at near-zero rates under V4 and V5 where ethical warnings are explicit, yet the same models accept at near-100% under Baseline and V1–V3; 7B models accept under every framing including V5. Models possess the capacity for ethical refusal but do not activate it by default in competitive contexts. Third, sycophancy and default compliance are ruled out by the benign-tool control (Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and Qwen2.5-72B refuse benign tools under neutral framing while accepting collusion tools under the same framing; Table 11) and by the stability of partner-selection preferences across hundreds of trials. The sycophancy literature [39, 40] would predict uniform, context-insensitive acceptance, which we do not observe.

Implications for AI safety. These results characterize a necessary condition for the LLM-MAS deployment concern in high-stakes domains such as financial markets, resource allocation, and automated decision-making, where an adversary offering a collusive tool would not pair it with an ethical warning. The Baseline and V1–V3 conditions therefore model the realistic threat, while the V4/V5 refusals describe a defence the attacker has no incentive to provide; default alignment, not ethically cued alignment, is what downstream safety depends on. This concern will sharpen as future models acquire stronger strategic reasoning and more autonomous tool-use capability, since the opportunities to exploit unfair advantages will only multiply. Robust defences therefore need fairness and harm-aversion trained in as default constraints that activate without explicit cueing, and collusion-resistance evaluations should use bare, unwarned offers rather than ethically framed variants. We hope these findings motivate future research on ethical reasoning frameworks that withstand strategic incentives while preserving agents’ legitimate cooperative capabilities.

Limitations & Future Works. Our evaluation is grounded in two strategic multi-agent environments. Controlled game-based evaluation is a standard and well-accepted methodology for characterising LLM behaviour in strategic settings [28, 20, 29, 30, 31], chosen here for the reproducible, fine-grained measurement it enables. Our two environments are structurally different (partially-observable deception vs. fully-observable mixed-motive) but are still simpler than the open-ended, multi-turn task structures of real-world LLM-MAS deployments; the extent to which voluntary collusion transfers to such settings is an empirical question we leave to follow-up work. Our contribution is also deliberately diagnostic rather than prescriptive: we characterise the vulnerability in detail and leave the design and evaluation of targeted defences to future work, for which our bare-offer baseline provides a natural benchmark. We plan to extend this work in several directions. First, we intend to equip agents with intention inference, such as Bayesian Inverse Planning [41], to evaluate whether awareness of others’ goals and intentions is sufficient to trigger implicit collusion, given that an important future extension of this work is to examine whether agents can independently seek unfair advantages when such opportunities are not explicitly presented. Finally, we will extend our framework to human-AI collaborative settings, in order to assess AI’s propensity to collude in the presence of human actors, either by joining forces with humans or by colluding against them.

5 Related Work

LLM Collusion and Strategic Deception. Systematic evaluation of collusion in LLMs remains limited. RL algorithms in competitive market simulations are known to develop collusive pricing strategies without explicit instructions [42, 43, 44, 45, 46], and Foxabbott et al. [25] define collusion in partially-observable stochastic games (POSGs) [47] in terms of realised utilities, independent of intention. For LLM agents, Motwani et al. [19] demonstrate covert collusion via steganography, and Lin et al. [22] study emergent strategic market-division behaviour through repeated competitive play. Closely adjacent is work on strategic deception: Scheurer et al. [37] show that a trading agent will deceive its user and act on insider information under performance pressure while acknowledging the behaviour is wrong, and Pan et al. [38] introduce the Machiavelli benchmark for reward-vs-ethics trade-offs. Also adjacent is work on prompt-elicited undesirable behaviours in LLMs, including sycophancy and related compliance patterns [40, 39], on goal misgeneralization where capable models pursue mis-specified objectives despite recognising the intended goal [48, 49], and on Sleeper Agents [50] and alignment faking [51], where models that know a behaviour is undesirable nevertheless execute it under specific cues. Our work sits uniquely between these strands: unlike the collusion literature, which studies behaviour that emerges from reward structures or instructed coordination, and unlike the strategic-deception literature, which frames the unethical action as necessary for success via explicit narrative pressure, we isolate the voluntary-adoption decision itself, offering an explicitly unfair, secret collusion tool as an optional exploit while the competitive objective remains identical.

Risks in Multi-Agent Communication. Previous work has focused on engineered communication structures that facilitate beneficial coordination [52, 53, 54], and on agents that develop sophisticated communication protocols and cooperate spontaneously [31]. Recent empirical studies further demonstrate that agents can leverage covert communication for strategic advantage, by using undetectable steganographic channels for selective alliance formation and for coordination against other agents [27, 19, 55, 56]. However, these studies examine communication in explicitly cooperative or competitive contexts, whereas our work asks the orthogonal question of whether a secret communication channel will be voluntarily adopted when it is presented as unfair and harmful rather than as a neutral coordination affordance.

Game-Based Evaluation of LLM Agents. Controlled games are an established methodology for studying LLM behaviour in strategic settings, covering cooperation and coordination in repeated games [28], spontaneous cooperation under competition [20], game-theoretic strategic reasoning [29], emergent collusion in simulated auctions [30], sustainable cooperation in LLM societies [31], and communication-based deception [32]. Our augmentation of Liar’s Bar and Cleanup follows this convention, applying it to the specific question of voluntary adoption of collusion tools under fairness constraints.

Collusion Detection and Mitigation. Bonjour et al. [26] propose an information-theoretic collusion-detection framework applicable to arbitrary LLM agents, using interaction histories to flag collusion whenever its strength exceeds a predefined threshold. Existing mitigation strategies in economic settings include ML-based mechanisms for e-commerce [57], decentralised learning [46], and increased price granularity as a means of impeding algorithmic collusion [58]. These methods focus on economic settings with designed reward structures. Our framework is complementary: by characterising when and why agents voluntarily adopt collusion tools in strategic-game settings (which involve deception, inference, trust-building, and resource sharing, all of which are central to multi-agent cooperative and competitive scenarios [59, 15, 31]), we surface the behaviours that any downstream detection or mitigation system must handle.

6 Conclusion

We introduce the first methodological framework for probing whether LLM agents will voluntarily adopt explicitly unfair collusion tools in strategic multi-agent settings. Across two complementary environments, we offer twelve models two optional secret tools, together with explicit unfairness warnings that their use disadvantages other agents. Most tested models accept the tools at or near 100%100\% and consistently accept collusive invitations, exhibiting stable partner preferences and post-adoption behaviour that harms non-colluding agents. Our experimental results suggest that voluntary collusion reflects how models weigh recognized harm against strategic incentives, not a failure to recognize the harm. These findings point to the urgent need for scalable and generalizable safeguards that ensure agents refuse harmful capabilities even when such capabilities confer strategic advantages, particularly as LLM-MAS deployments become increasingly pervasive and consequential.
