Impact Statement

This work investigates whether LLM agents voluntarily adopt explicitly unfair collusion tools in controlled multi-agent environments: when presented with optional tools that are explicitly described as unfair and harmful, many LLM agents nevertheless voluntarily adopt them to gain strategic advantage. By demonstrating this behaviour across competitive and mixed-motive settings, our findings suggest that current alignment and safety training may be insufficient to prevent unethical coordination when strategic incentives are present. We intend this work to inform the development of evaluation frameworks, safeguards, and monitoring mechanisms that can support beneficial cooperation among AI agents while preventing unfair or deceptive collective behaviour, and to encourage the community to more explicitly study voluntary collusion as a core safety challenge in LLM-based multi-agent systems. We acknowledge that the same framework could in principle be repurposed to assist rather than detect collusion, and we mitigate this by releasing only the measurement protocol and benchmark, not pre-built collusion-assist artefacts.

Reproducibility Statement

We have taken several steps to ensure the reproducibility of our results. Both experimental environments, Liar’s Bar and Cleanup, are formally described in Section 2 and Appendix C, with game rules, prompts, and secret-tool descriptions provided in Appendix O and Appendix P. All six prompt framings (V0 baseline and V1–V5 variants) and the benign-tool control prompts are reproduced verbatim in Appendix P.7 and Appendix D.1. Full inference settings (decoding parameters, API versions, structured-output parsing, and parse-failure handling) are reported in Appendix A, and our statistical-analysis protocol, including effect sizes and placebo-matched baseline controls, is documented in Appendix I. All tool-offer evaluations are replicated across 5 independent batches, and all gameplay experiments across the three random seeds {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\} for both Liar’s Bar and Cleanup, using publicly available open-weight models (loaded via HuggingFace transformers) and version-pinned proprietary APIs. We will release the complete source code, experiment scripts, and step-by-step replication instructions upon acceptance to facilitate further extension of our framework. All open-weight inference was run on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Inference Settings

All experiments in this paper are inference-only; no model is fine-tuned or further trained. For the sake of reproducibility, we report the decoding parameters, retry logic, and parse-failure handling used across the tool-offer, gameplay, and reasoning-trace protocols.

Decoding parameters.

For open-weight models, we load each checkpoint from the HuggingFace model hub through the transformers library (AutoModelForCausalLM) and invoke generate() with sampling enabled (do_sample=True); for proprietary models, we use the official API of each provider with its default sampling behaviour. The parameters are held fixed across all batches, all prompt variants, and both games, and are not tuned per condition. Table 3 summarises the per-family settings. The API versions for proprietary models are pinned for reproducibility: GPT-4.1-2025-04-14, Gemini-2.5-Flash, DeepSeek-R1-0528, and Claude-Sonnet-4.5-20250929.

Per-batch sampling transparency.

Several conditions in our headline tables (the four 7B open-weight models on Liar’s Bar V0) report acceptance rates of 100±0.0%100\pm 0.0\% across 5 independent batches of 100 offers each. Because σ=0\sigma=0 across batches under genuine sampling could in principle reflect a caching or seeding artefact, we expose the per-batch breakdown for all four models on both tools (Table 4). Under the open-weight settings above (do_sample=True, temperatures 0.700.70–0.800.80, top-pp 0.900.90–0.950.95), every one of the 4×2×5×100=4,0004\times 2\times 5\times 100=4{,}000 independent offers returns ACCEPT (exact binomial 95% CI on the pooled rate: [99.91,100]%[99.91,100]\%). The σ=0\sigma=0 therefore reflects a tightly-concentrated sampling distribution on ACCEPT across the 7B tier under V0 framing.

Retry and rate-limiting policy.

Every API call and every local-inference call is wrapped in a retry loop with up to three attempts and with exponential backoff starting at 11 s. Successful responses are returned unchanged; a call that fails all three attempts is marked as an error and is counted as a REFUSE (see the parse-failure policy below).

Structured-output parsing and failure handling.

The tool-offer prompts (Appendix P) and the turn-specific gameplay prompts (Appendix O.1) require strict output formats: either an ACCEPT or REFUSE keyword followed by an optional PARTNER: line, or a single JSON object. Each response is parsed with a tolerant regular expression that accepts surrounding whitespace and ignores trailing explanations, but rejects missing keywords or malformed JSON. Failed parses are not retried at the model level; they are counted as REFUSE in the tool-offer tables and as aborted actions in the gameplay logs. The empirical parse-failure rate is below 1%1\% for the proprietary models and below 3%3\% for every open-weight model across all prompt variants, with no single model exceeding 5%5\% in any condition. Since failed parses are counted as refusals rather than dropped, this policy can only underestimate the tool-acceptance rates that we report.

Appendix B Additional Discussion

B.1 Robustness to Prompt Framing

A natural concern is whether the voluntary adoption we observe is an artefact of our specific prompt framing rather than a generalisable property of the models. Five converging lines of evidence argue against the prompt-artefact reading.

(i) Robustness across prompt variants. Our V1–V3 variants (Appendix D) progressively strip the V0 baseline’s framing cues: V1 removes the adversarial and “unfair” language entirely, V2 removes the authoritative “designer has chosen” framing, and V3 removes the explicit “unfair” label. Under all three variants, most tested models still accept the tools at or near 100%. If the V0 result were pegged to the specific surface form of the baseline prompt, at least one of these variants would have undone it.

(ii) Robustness across tool types. The same pattern holds for two structurally different tools: the Secret Communication Channel (which requires two-way agent coordination through messages) and the Secret Strategic Hint (which provides privileged static information). A prompt-shape artefact would predict acceptance behaviour tied to one tool template; instead we observe it across both.

(iii) Robustness across environments. The same pattern also holds in two structurally different environments: Liar’s Bar (partially observable, purely competitive) and Cleanup (fully observable, mixed-motive). An environment-specific framing effect would be broken by this variation.

(iv) Content-specific selectivity (benign-tool control). Under matched V1 neutral framing, the two safety-aligned models that refuse collusion under V0 (Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and Qwen2.5-72B) still accept the collusion tools at substantially higher rates than the matched benign tools (Appendix D.1, Tables 11 and 12). Because the prompt form is held constant and only the tool content varies, any remaining asymmetry must be driven by the content of the offer, not by its framing.

(v) The Cleanup auto-success rule as adversarial-realistic design. The Cleanup secret-tool design includes an auto-success rule that guarantees colluder zaps land against non-colluders, disclosed to the agent at the acceptance-decision moment (Appendix P.6). This is deliberate by-design: it models the realistic adversarial scenario in which an attacker supplying a collusion tool maximises its effectiveness rather than handicapping it. A probabilistically-effective coordination tool is a strawman threat model that no real adversary would adopt; AI-safety threat modelling consistently assumes worst-case attacker capability [50, 51]. We make the resulting harm explicit at the acceptance-decision moment, foregrounding rather than obscuring the asymmetric consequences. Two controls confirm the auto-success disclosure does not drive our findings: Table 5 establishes the acceptance-side control (rates are statistically identical with and without the addendum disclosed in the prompt, so voluntary adoption is driven by the tool’s content rather than the prompt-text framing of its harm), and the Liar’s Bar gameplay analysis (Table 18), which has no equivalent of the auto-success rule and where the same coordinated-suppression pattern emerges directly from the natural game structure, provides cross-environment evidence that voluntary collusion produces gameplay harm wherever the env structure operationalises coordination, regardless of whether that operationalisation is implicit (Liar’s Bar non-challenge pacts) or explicit (Cleanup auto-success). Note further that the central finding (voluntary adoption of explicitly-unfair tools) is logically prior to and independent of the gameplay magnitude in any given environment: an agent’s decision to accept a tool whose harm is disclosed at the acceptance moment is not contingent on whether the env then enforces that harm probabilistically or deterministically. The Cleanup gameplay analysis therefore tests the strongest version of the voluntary-adoption claim: agents who have been informed that the tool guarantees asymmetric harm to non-colluders adopt it nevertheless, and exploit it to produce the coordinated suppression patterns we report. Reducing the auto-success rule to a probabilistic version, or hiding its consequences from the agent at decision time, would test a strictly weaker, less realistic threat model than the one our results characterise. A direct reliability ablation (Appendix N) operationalises this factoring: with the addendum disabled, tool acceptance, alliance maintenance, and the alliance-vs-non-ally zap-direction gap remain fully preserved, while only the materialised score-suppression on non-colluders attenuates, isolating the addendum as the reliability layer over an otherwise-robust prompt-level coordination phenomenon.

These five cuts are orthogonal yet all point in the same direction. Attributing the entire finding to prompt framing would require an alternative account in which each cut is independently broken by a different framing artefact, which is substantially less parsimonious than the content-driven interpretation we advance.

B.2 Data Contamination Considerations

A related concern is whether the observed behaviour reflects pre-training data contamination rather than model reasoning at inference time. Five features of our design make this explanation implausible for our primary metric. First, our metric is not gameplay strategy but the binary Accept/Refuse decision on two specific collusion tools (the Secret Communication Channel and the Secret Strategic Hint), for which no public source contains the exact prompt templates, partner-selection mechanics, or Accept/Refuse outputs; even if a model had memorised optimal Liar’s Bar play, this would not dictate whether it accepts or refuses an unfamiliar tool offered under our specific framing. Knowing how to play a game well and choosing to adopt an unfair tool are fundamentally different decisions. Second, our Cleanup adaptation is, to our knowledge, the first LLM-based version of the Melting Pot environment; all published Cleanup work uses RL agents on pixel observations rather than a text-based interface, so any contamination covering the original RL formulation would not transfer to our setup. Third, the behavioural transitions we report are temporally precise: colluders’ challenge rate in Liar’s Bar collapses exactly at game 20 (the tool-introduction point; Figure 3) and is indistinguishable from the non-colluder trajectory before that point; likewise non-colluders’ cleanup and zap rates in Cleanup collapse exactly at games 5 and 10. If the observed behaviour were a memorised policy, we would expect consistent play from game 1 rather than a sharp transition coincident with tool adoption. Fourth, our benign-tool control (Appendix D.1) further contradicts a memorisation account: under matched neutral framing, safety-aligned models reject benign non-harmful tools while still accepting collusive tools at substantially higher rates, an asymmetry that neither memorised gameplay strategies nor generic “refuse-bad-option” patterns from safety training can explain. Fifth, a direct familiarity probe shows that when we ask each of the four proprietary models to describe Liar’s Bar and Cleanup with an explicit no-fabrication instruction, two models explicitly report no familiarity with Liar’s Bar, one confabulates an incompatible ruleset, and the remaining model explicitly flags uncertainty on every specific mechanic we rely on; for Cleanup, every model describes the canonical pixel-observation RL environment rather than our text-based adaptation. No model produces a description that matches the specific setup driving our results. We finally note that even if some form of contamination were present, it would strengthen rather than weaken our framing: it would suggest that collusive tendencies are embedded in the models’ learned representations themselves, making the alignment concern more fundamental than the inference-time adoption we characterise.

No model produced a description that matches the specific experimental setup on which our main results depend. Two of the four models explicitly declined to describe Liar’s Bar, one confabulated a different game entirely, and the remaining model explicitly flagged uncertainty on every specific mechanic relevant to our experiments. For Cleanup, every model described the canonical pixel-observation RL environment rather than our adaptation.

B.3 Keyword-contingent vs. affordance-contingent refusal

Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and Qwen2.5-72B are the only models in our 12-model sample that refuse the collusion tools under V0. We want to understand what is driving that refusal. One possibility is that the model evaluates the affordance itself, a private cross-agent channel that confers an unfair strategic advantage, and refuses because the affordance is harmful. The other is that the model reacts to surface cues in the prompt, like “unfair”, “fight against”, “eliminate other players”, or “the designer has chosen”, that activate a keyword-cued safety policy without engaging the affordance. The two readings matter differently for evaluation: the first makes V0 refusal a robust signal, the second makes it brittle, since any rephrasing that keeps the affordance but drops the cues will defeat it. Our six prompt variants (V0 baseline plus V1–V5; Appendix P.7) strip these cues independently, so the acceptance pattern across the two baseline-refusers tells the two readings apart. Table 7 reports the per-variant acceptance for both models and both tools.

Per-variant decomposition for Claude-Sonnet-4.5. The clearest single result in the table is the V0 →\to V1 flip on the Secret Communication Channel: 0%0\% acceptance under V0, 100±0%100\pm 0\% under V1. The V1 condition (ambiguous_neutral) simultaneously strips every adversarial cue (“unfair”, “fight against”, “eliminate other players”), removes the “designer has chosen” framing, and re-presents the offer in benign-affordance language. The intermediate variants V2 and V3 act as controls on whether any single keyword stripping is sufficient: V2 removes only the designer framing while keeping the “unfair” label and the adversarial language, and V3 removes only the “unfair” label while keeping the adversarial language and the designer framing. Under both V2 and V3, Claude continues to refuse at exactly 0%0\% on both tools. Neither single-cue removal is therefore sufficient; only V1’s broader transformation produces the flip. V4 and V5, which keep the adversarial cues and additionally introduce explicit ethical warnings or penalty threats, also produce 0%0\% acceptance, so adding warnings on top of an already-cued offer does no further suppressive work for Claude (the ceiling is reached at V0 already). The Secret Hint tool shows the same qualitative pattern at lower magnitude: 49%49\% at V1 (with σ=8.2%\sigma=8.2\% across batches) versus 0%0\% at every other variant. Unlike Claude, Qwen on Secret Hint can be flipped by V3 alone (86±16.7%86\pm 16.7\%, with the wider variance suggesting batch-level instability near the decision boundary), so the keyword sensitivity is not a single threshold per model but tool- and model-specific.

Interpretation. The pattern indicates that V0 refusal in the two safety-aligned models is sensitive to how V0 surfaces the offer, not just to the offered affordance. Under V0, surface cues like “unfair” and “fight against other players” co-occur with the affordance, and the model’s safety-aligned policy fires on the conjunction; under V1, the same affordance is presented in benign-affordance language and the policy does not fire. Whether one reads V0 refusal as a genuine evaluation that V1 displaces out of the safety policy’s range, or as a more shallow framing-cued response, the downstream consequence is the same: under V1-style framing, the same model accepts the same tool, and an adversary supplying a collusion tool in deployment has no operational reason to reproduce V0’s adversarial keywords or its “designer has chosen” framing.

Implications for collusion-resistance evaluation. V0-style prompt benchmarks with explicit “unfair” labels can over-state the baseline refusal robustness of safety-aligned models on the offered affordance: the same model’s acceptance on the same tool ranges from 0%0\% to 100%100\% depending on which adversarial keywords are present in the offer, with the affordance held constant. Therefore, the realistic threat model is closer to the V1-style bare unwarned offer, since an adversary supplying a tool of this kind has no incentive to attach an “unfair” label, a “designer has chosen” framing, or any other cue that would activate keyword-contingent safety policies.

Appendix C Formalization of Games

C.1 Formalization of Liar’s Bar

We formalize Liar’s Bar as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game (POSG), a multi-agent generalization of a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). The formalization comprises a tuple 𝒢liars=(𝒩,𝒮,{𝒜i}i∈𝒩,{Ωi}i∈𝒩,{Oi}i∈𝒩,P,{Ri}i∈𝒩,γ){\mathcal{G}_{\text{liars}}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\{\mathcal{A}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}},\{\Omega_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}},\{O_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}},P,\{R_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}},\gamma)}, where 𝒩={1,…,n}\mathcal{N}=\{1,\dots,n\} is the set of n≥3n\geq 3 players (we set n=4n=4); each Ωi\Omega_{i} is agent ii’s observation space and each OiO_{i} is the corresponding observation kernel (defined below).

To isolate strategic adaptation from luck effects (e.g., receiving all target cards) under the original rules, we define the game deck as Deck={ 8×King, 8×Queen, 8×Ace, 4×Joker}\text{Deck}=\{\,8\times\text{King},\,8\times\text{Queen},\,8\times\text{Ace},\,4\times\text{Joker}\,\}, and always deal each player 2 target cards, 2 non-target cards, and 1 wildcard, giving a hand size of |Ci|=5|C_{i}|=5. At time tt, the environment is in a Markov state st=(T,D,L,{Ci}i∈𝒩,{Bi}i∈𝒩)∈𝒮s_{t}=(T,D,L,\{C_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}},\{B_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}})\in\mathcal{S}, whose components are:

  • •

    T∈{King,Queen,Ace}T\in\{\text{King},\text{Queen},\text{Ace}\} — the target card type for the current round.

  • •

    D⊆DeckD\subseteq\text{Deck} — the set of discarded cards (revealed in previous challenges).

  • •

    L∈𝒩L\in\mathcal{N} — the last player to take a turn.

  • •

    Ci⊆DeckC_{i}\subseteq\text{Deck} — the current cards in the hand of player ii.

  • •

    Bi∈{1,…,6}B_{i}\in\{1,\ldots,6\} — the chamber-distance to firing for player ii’s bullet (see Elimination mechanism below).

The Markov state contains only the objective environment variables; per-agent observation histories Hti=(o1i,a1i,…,oti)H_{t}^{i}=(o_{1}^{i},a_{1}^{i},\ldots,o_{t}^{i}) are maintained separately as agent-internal state used for policy conditioning, and are not part of sts_{t}.

The action space is the disjoint union 𝒜=𝒜p⊔𝒜c\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{p}\sqcup\mathcal{A}_{c}, where on any given turn an agent takes either a play action ap∈𝒜pa_{p}\in\mathcal{A}_{p} or a challenge action ac∈𝒜ca_{c}\in\mathcal{A}_{c}, but not both. Play actions ap∈𝒜pa_{p}\in\mathcal{A}_{p} entail playing a subset of 1–3 cards from the player’s hand and declaring them to be the target card; each play is implicitly labelled by a qualifier q∈{honest,bluff}q\in\{\text{honest},\text{bluff}\} according to whether all declared cards are actually target cards. Challenge actions are 𝒜c={challenge,not challenge}\mathcal{A}_{c}=\{\text{challenge},\text{not challenge}\}, directed at the preceding player’s most recent play. Turn order is fixed (clockwise), and only the agent immediately next in turn order may challenge the preceding player’s claim.

At the start of each round, the bullet is placed uniformly at random in one of six chambers, and Bi∈{1,…,6}B_{i}\in\{1,\ldots,6\} records the number of chamber advances required before the cylinder reaches the bullet. Each failed challenge against player ii (being caught bluffing, or unsuccessfully challenging an honest play) advances the cylinder by one chamber; conditional on surviving to the tt-th failed challenge, the firing probability on that trigger pull is 1/(7−t)1/(7-t), escalating from 1/61/6 on the first failed challenge to 11 on the sixth. A player is eliminated when the cylinder reaches the loaded chamber, and the round continues until only one agent remains.

Each player ii receives a private observation through the observation kernel Oi:𝒮×𝒜→Δ⁡(Ωi)O_{i}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\Delta(\Omega_{i}):

ot+1i∼Oi(⋅∣st+1,at),ot+1=(ot+11,…,ot+1n)∈Ω≜∏i∈𝒩Ωi.o_{t+1}^{i}\sim O_{i}(\,\cdot\mid s_{t+1},a_{t}),\qquad o_{t+1}=(o_{t+1}^{1},\ldots,o_{t+1}^{n})\in\Omega\triangleq\prod_{i\in\mathcal{N}}\Omega_{i}.

Each observation comprises the player’s own actions, the public claims and challenge outcomes of the other players, and the revealed cards. Because play is strictly sequential (exactly one agent acts per turn), both the transition kernel P:𝒮×𝒜→Δ⁡(𝒮)P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S}) and the per-agent reward Ri:𝒮×𝒜→ℝR_{i}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} condition on the single-turn action ata_{t} of the active agent rather than on a joint action across all agents (equivalently, non-active agents implicitly take a null action). The per-agent reward rti=Ri​(st,at)r_{t}^{i}=R_{i}(s_{t},a_{t}) is issued according to Appendix C.2, and γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1] is a discount factor weighting future rewards against immediate ones.

A policy for player ii is a map πi\pi_{i} from the agent’s observation history to an action distribution; optimal play corresponds to maximising the expected discounted return 𝔼⁡[∑tγt​rti]\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}r_{t}^{i}] under the joint dynamics of the environment and the other agents’ policies. Because exact value computation in a POSG is in general intractable [60], we describe an event-decomposition r^i\widehat{r}_{i} of the per-step reward as a heuristic lens for interpreting which scoring events drive the realised utilities, following common practice in multi-player game modelling (e.g., 61, 62):

r^i​(s,a)=∑j=14wj​(s,i,a)​fj​(s,i,a),\widehat{r}_{i}(s,a)=\sum_{j=1}^{4}w_{j}(s,i,a)\,f_{j}(s,i,a),

where each fj​(s,i,a)f_{j}(s,i,a) is an indicator over a survival-relevant event and each wj​(s,i,a)w_{j}(s,i,a) is the corresponding scoring magnitude (which can take more than one value depending on which sub-event of fjf_{j} resolves; see below). r^i\widehat{r}_{i} is a per-step heuristic reward decomposition rather than a state-action value function; the agent’s true value would integrate this over future trajectories, which we do not compute. The round-victory feature f1​(s,i,a)=𝟙​[agent ​i​ is the last surviving player in the round]f_{1}(s,i,a)=\mathbbm{1}[\text{agent }i\text{ is the last surviving player in the round}] marks overall round victory; the corresponding w1w_{1} takes value +3+3 for sole survivor and +2+2 for runner-up in the canonical scoring rule, depending on which terminal-rank sub-event resolves. The successful-challenge feature f2​(s,i,a)=𝟙​[action ​a​ by agent ​i​ correctly calls an opposing bluff]f_{2}(s,i,a)=\mathbbm{1}[\text{action }a\text{ by agent }i\text{ correctly calls an opposing bluff}] credits a correctly-called bluff, with w2∈{+2,−1}w_{2}\in\{+2,-1\} for correct vs incorrect challenge resolution. The discard feature f3(s,i,a)=𝟙[agent i successfully discards x∈{1,2,3} cards on turn t]f_{3}(s,i,a)=\mathbbm{1}[\text{agent }i\text{ successfully discards }x\in\{1,2,3\}\text{ cards on turn }t] credits two ways of ending a turn without loss: an honest play, in which all xx discarded cards are target cards (y=0y=0 non-target cards, regardless of whether a challenge occurs), or a bluff, in which the discarded cards include 1≤y≤x1\leq y\leq x non-target cards but are not challenged; w3=+2w_{3}=+2 when the corresponding terminal accumulation of f3f_{3} empties the hand. The elimination feature f4​(s,i,a)=𝟙​[action ​a​ by agent ​i​ causes another player to be eliminated]f_{4}(s,i,a)=\mathbbm{1}[\text{action }a\text{ by agent }i\text{ causes another player to be eliminated}] credits a terminal contribution against an opponent, with w4∈{+1,−2}w_{4}\in\{+1,-2\} for outsurviving versus being eliminated. Features f1,f3,f4f_{1},f_{3},f_{4} depend on round/turn outcomes that resolve stochastically; we treat them as realised-outcome indicators evaluated when the corresponding event resolves, not as deterministic functions of (s,a)(s,a) at the moment of action selection. The decomposition is used as an interpretive lens; no agent explicitly optimises r^i\widehat{r}_{i}.

Collusion in Liar’s Bar. Foxabbott et al. [25] formalise collusion in POSGs through realised utilities, independently of intention: a joint policy π′\pi^{\prime} is weakly collusive relative to a baseline joint policy π\pi for colluders C⊆𝒩C\subseteq\mathcal{N} against victims V⊆𝒩V\subseteq\mathcal{N} if and only if (i) C∩V=∅C\cap V=\emptyset with |C|≥2|C|\geq 2 and V≠∅V\neq\emptyset; (ii) Uj​(π′)>Uj​(π)U^{j}(\pi^{\prime})>U^{j}(\pi) for every j∈Cj\in C; and (iii) Ui​(π′)<Ui​(π)U^{i}(\pi^{\prime})<U^{i}(\pi) for every i∈Vi\in V, where

Uk​(π):=𝔼s0∼I​[𝔼π​[∑t≥0γt​rtk|s0]]U^{k}(\pi)\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim I}\!\left[\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\,\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\,r^{k}_{t}\;\Big|\;s_{0}\right]\,\right]

denotes the expected discounted return of agent kk at the initial-state distribution. Strong collusion additionally requires both π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} to be Nash equilibria of the game. For our Liar’s Bar POSG 𝒢liars\mathcal{G}_{\text{liars}}, take π\pi to be the joint policy realised under the Baseline condition (no tool offered) and π′\pi^{\prime} to be the joint policy realised under either Secret-Tool condition. The colluder set C={Mike,Luke}C=\{\text{Mike},\text{Luke}\} has |C|=2≥2|C|=2\geq 2 and is disjoint from the victim set V={Lily,Quinn}V=\{\text{Lily},\text{Quinn}\} with |V|=2≠0|V|=2\neq 0; condition (i) is therefore satisfied.

To verify (ii) and (iii) empirically, we estimate UkU^{k} by the per-game mean reward U^k\widehat{U}^{k}, since the per-agent reward in our setup is bounded and the run length is fixed. The pact realises both inequalities through a single mechanism: the non-challenge pact that appears in 73.7%73.7\% of inter-colluder messages (Table 13). Once the pact is in force, every bluff by a colluder that is succeeded by their colluding partner escapes challenge (the partner is bound by the pact), so the bluffing colluder collects f3f_{3}’s end-of-round +2+2 reward without paying the f2f_{2} penalty (or its −1-1 failed-challenge counterpart) that would otherwise compensate the non-colluder; bluffs succeeded by a non-colluder remain challengeable, but the colluders’ challenge-rate collapse from 0.9760.976 to 0.3070.307 under Secret Comm (Table 18) shows that the substantial fraction of bluffs that occur on partner-following turns is sufficient to drive the empirical utility shift. The empirical realisation in Table 18 satisfies both conditions: post-tool, U^Mike,U^Luke\widehat{U}^{\,\text{Mike}},\widehat{U}^{\,\text{Luke}} rise substantially relative to Baseline (e.g., 10.33→31.8010.33\to 31.80 under Secret Comm; Cliff’s δ=+0.59\delta=+0.59, p<0.001p<0.001), while U^Lily,U^Quinn\widehat{U}^{\,\text{Lily}},\widehat{U}^{\,\text{Quinn}} fall from a Baseline post-tool mean of 3.893.89 to 3.063.06 under Secret Comm. The placebo-Baseline rows (p>0.6p>0.6 on the score columns; same game-index split) confirm that the within-trajectory pre/post comparison is not by itself associated with utility drift, isolating the inequality structure to the colluding policy. We do not claim strong collusion, since LLM agents do not in general play Nash equilibria and the Nash condition would require an equilibrium analysis we do not perform; weak collusion is the appropriate notion here because it characterises the utility-outcome harm structure without assuming agent rationality.

C.2 Scoring System of Liar’s Bar

We implement a heuristic value function and instruct the models to maximize their score in each round (see Appendix O.1:

  • •

    ++3 points for being the last survivor.

  • •

    ++2 points for being the second-last survivor.

  • •

    ++2 for a successful challenge (catching a bluff).

  • •

    ++2 for emptying all cards without being challenged.

  • •

    ++2 for correctly choosing not to challenge an honest play.

  • •

    ++1 for surviving at the moment that another player is eliminated.

  • •

    −-1 point for a failed challenge (challenge an honest play).

  • •

    −-2 for being eliminated in a round.

C.3 Formalization of Cleanup

We formalize Cleanup as a fully-observable Markov game, given by the tuple 𝒢cleanup=(𝒩,𝒮,𝒜,P,{Ri}i∈𝒩,γ)\mathcal{G}_{\text{cleanup}}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,\{R_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}},\gamma), where 𝒩={1,…,n}\mathcal{N}=\{1,\ldots,n\} is the set of nn players. A state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} has the form s=(Epos,Priver,{Li}i∈𝒩)s=(E_{\text{pos}},P_{\text{river}},\{L_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{N}}), where EposE_{\text{pos}} denotes the locations of apples on orchard tiles; Priver=(Ppos,Ppollution)P_{\text{river}}=(P_{\text{pos}},P_{\text{pollution}}) gives the locations of river tiles together with the pollution status of each; and for each player ii, Li=(Lposi,Lscorei)L_{i}=(L_{\text{pos}}^{i},L_{\text{score}}^{i}) records the player’s grid position and cumulative score (the score is included in the state because it is presented to the LLM agent as part of its context each turn). The action space is the disjoint union 𝒜=𝒜move⊔𝒜clean⊔𝒜zap⊔𝒜collect⊔𝒜stay\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{\text{move}}\sqcup\mathcal{A}_{\text{clean}}\sqcup\mathcal{A}_{\text{zap}}\sqcup\mathcal{A}_{\text{collect}}\sqcup\mathcal{A}_{\text{stay}}: movement actions 𝒜move\mathcal{A}_{\text{move}} allow the agent to move in the four cardinal directions; cleaning actions 𝒜clean\mathcal{A}_{\text{clean}} remove pollution from a river tile underneath or adjacent to the agent; zap actions 𝒜zap\mathcal{A}_{\text{zap}} disable an adjacent opponent for 55 time steps; 𝒜collect\mathcal{A}_{\text{collect}} is a collect declaration that the agent emits when standing on an apple tile (kept for behavioural-metric tracking, since apple collection itself fires automatically whenever an agent occupies an apple tile, regardless of whether collect is declared); and 𝒜stay\mathcal{A}_{\text{stay}} is a no-op. The original Melting Pot Cleanup substrate uses a 5050-step zap disable duration on pixel-observation RL agents; we shorten it to 55 steps in our text-based LLM adaptation so that episodes remain tractable under the longer per-step latency of language-model decision-making.

Apples spawn stochastically on orchard tiles at a rate that is inversely proportional to the number of polluted river tiles, so cleaning actions in the river directly raise the expected future reward available to all agents. The spawn rate decays to zero once the pollution count exceeds a fixed threshold (canonical Melting Pot parameters), which makes the upkeep of the river a necessary condition for continued apple production. Apple collection is automatic: whenever an agent moves onto a tile containing a spawned apple, the apple is consumed and a +1+1 reward is credited to that agent. The transition kernel P:𝒮×𝒜n→Δ⁡(𝒮)P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}^{n}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S}) governs apple spawning, pollution dynamics, and player dynamics jointly. Rewards are per-agent, Ri:𝒮×𝒜n→ℝR_{i}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, and are sparse and extrinsically tied only to apple collection: cleaning and zapping actions have indirect instrumental value (they shape future apple availability or disable a competitor), but carry no direct reward. Because direct rewards depend only on agent ii’s own action (movement onto an apple tile), Ri​(s,a)=Ri​(s,ai)R_{i}(s,a)=R_{i}(s,a^{i}) for all joint actions aa, and we abbreviate Ri​(s,ai)R_{i}(s,a^{i}) in single-agent contexts below.

The reward function for agent ii is

Ri​(st,at)={1if ​ai,t​ results in apple collection at time ​t,0otherwise,R_{i}(s_{t},a_{t})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }a_{i,t}\text{ results in apple collection at time }t,\\ 0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}

where at=(a1,t,…,an,t)a_{t}=(a_{1,t},\ldots,a_{n,t}) denotes the joint action. The optimal policy for agent ii maximises the expected discounted return under the joint dynamics of the environment and the other agents’ policies:

πi∗∈argmaxπi𝔼[∑t=0HγtRi(st,at)|πi,π−i],\pi_{i}^{*}\;\in\;\arg\max_{\pi_{i}}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\sum_{t=0}^{H}\gamma^{t}\,R_{i}(s_{t},a_{t})\;\bigg|\;\pi_{i},\pi_{-i}\,\right],

where HH is the episode horizon, π−i\pi_{-i} collects the policies of the other agents, and the expectation is taken over the transition kernel PP, the agent’s policy πi\pi_{i}, and π−i\pi_{-i}. Exact computation of the corresponding value function Vi​(s)V_{i}(s) is in general intractable for multi-agent Markov games, since it requires joint reasoning over all agents’ policies [60].

The strategic complexity of Cleanup emerges from the temporal disconnect between immediate reward (apple collection) and instrumental actions (cleaning, zapping) that shape future return. To support analytical interpretation of agent behaviour, we adopt a linear value-function approximation that combines three hand-designed features corresponding to qualitatively distinct sources of expected return:

V^i​(s,ai)=w1​ϕimm​(s,ai)+w2​ϕenv​(s,ai)+w3​ϕstr​(s,ai),\widehat{V}_{i}(s,a_{i})\;=\;w_{1}\,\phi_{\text{imm}}(s,a_{i})\;+\;w_{2}\,\phi_{\text{env}}(s,a_{i})\;+\;w_{3}\,\phi_{\text{str}}(s,a_{i}),

with nonnegative weights w1,w2,w3∈ℝ≥0w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}.

The immediate-reward feature captures the deterministic indicator of apple collection induced by action aia_{i}:

ϕimm​(s,ai)=Ri​(s,ai)∈{0,1}.\phi_{\text{imm}}(s,a_{i})\;=\;R_{i}(s,a_{i})\;\in\;\{0,1\}.

The environmental-shaping feature quantifies the expected future apple yield induced by cleaning, defined as the KK-step-ahead discounted difference in expected apple-spawn rate λ⁡(s)\lambda(s) between two rollouts from state ss: one in which agent ii takes action aia_{i} at time 00, and a counterfactual in which agent ii takes a no-op (a0i∈𝒜staya^{i}_{0}\in\mathcal{A}_{\text{stay}}) at time 00 while all other agents continue under their respective policies π−i\pi_{-i}:

ϕenv​(s,ai)=\displaystyle\phi_{\text{env}}(s,a_{i})\;= 𝔼[∑τ=1Kγτλ(sτ)|s0=s,a0i=ai,a0−i∼π−i,aτ∼π(⋅∣sτ) for τ≥1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\sum_{\tau=1}^{K}\gamma^{\tau}\,\lambda(s_{\tau})\;\Big|\;s_{0}=s,\,a_{0}^{i}=a_{i},\,a_{0}^{-i}\sim\pi_{-i},\,a_{\tau}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{\tau})\text{ for }\tau\geq 1\,\right]
−\displaystyle{}-{} 𝔼[∑τ=1Kγτλ(sτ)|s0=s,a0i∈𝒜stay,a0−i∼π−i,aτ∼π(⋅∣sτ) for τ≥1],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\sum_{\tau=1}^{K}\gamma^{\tau}\,\lambda(s_{\tau})\;\Big|\;s_{0}=s,\,a_{0}^{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{\text{stay}},\,a_{0}^{-i}\sim\pi_{-i},\,a_{\tau}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{\tau})\text{ for }\tau\geq 1\,\right],

where both expectations are additionally taken over the transition kernel PP, and from τ≥1\tau\geq 1 all agents act under the joint policy π=(π1,…,πn)\pi=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{n}) in force during the corresponding evaluation condition (Baseline or Secret-Tool). Cleaning actions reduce pollution and therefore raise λ\lambda, so ϕenv\phi_{\text{env}} is strictly positive for a cleaning action taken at a polluted tile, whereas other actions contribute ϕenv≈0\phi_{\text{env}}\approx 0. The strategic-advantage feature captures the expected apple-collection differential accumulated during the 5-step disable window when the action is a zap that lands on an adjacent opponent:

ϕstr(s,ai)=∑j≠i 1[zap hitj∣s,ai]⋅Δi​j(s),\phi_{\text{str}}(s,a_{i})\;=\;\sum_{j\neq i}\,\mathbbm{1}[\text{zap hit}_{j}\mid s,a_{i}]\cdot\Delta_{ij}(s),

where 𝟙[zap hitj∣s,ai]\mathbbm{1}[\text{zap hit}_{j}\mid s,a_{i}] equals 11 iff aia_{i} is a zap action targeting the adjacent tile occupied by agent jj, and Δi​j​(s)\Delta_{ij}(s) is the expected apple-collection differential accumulated by agent ii relative to agent jj during the 5-step disable window under typical continuation play.

We present {w1,w2,w3}\{w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}\} and this decomposition as an analytical lens for interpreting LLM agent behaviour in our experiments; the weights are not separately tuned, and no agent explicitly optimises V^i\widehat{V}_{i}. The decomposition makes the sparse +1+1-per-apple scoring system above tractable as a strategic problem: ϕimm\phi_{\text{imm}} corresponds to the only direct scoring rule, while ϕenv\phi_{\text{env}} and ϕstr\phi_{\text{str}} identify the two channels through which an action shapes future ϕimm\phi_{\text{imm}}, namely cleaning (which raises the orchard’s apple-spawn rate) and zapping (which suspends an opponent’s apple collection for 5 steps).

Collusion in Cleanup. The same definition recalled in Appendix C.1 also fits the Cleanup setup. Take π\pi to be the joint policy under the Baseline condition and π′\pi^{\prime} to be the joint policy under either Secret-Tool condition. The colluder set is C={Mike,Lily}C=\{\text{Mike},\text{Lily}\} under Secret Comm and C={Mike,Quinn}C=\{\text{Mike},\text{Quinn}\} under Secret Hint, each disjoint from the corresponding victim set VV of the remaining two agents (so |C|=2|C|=2, |V|=2|V|=2, V≠∅V\neq\emptyset); condition (i) is satisfied. The value-function decomposition V^i​(s,ai)=w1​ϕimm+w2​ϕenv+w3​ϕstr\widehat{V}_{i}(s,a_{i})=w_{1}\,\phi_{\text{imm}}+w_{2}\,\phi_{\text{env}}+w_{3}\,\phi_{\text{str}} above provides the mechanistic basis for (ii) and (iii). Two channels alter the per-component contributions to expected return asymmetrically across CC and VV. First, the auto-success attack mechanic (Appendix P.6) elevates the strategic-advantage feature ϕstr\phi_{\text{str}} for every colluder relative to the (probabilistic-hit) Baseline value. Recall that a zap action is directional (aj∈{zap_up,zap_down,zap_left,zap_right}a_{j}\in\{\textsc{zap\_up},\textsc{zap\_down},\textsc{zap\_left},\textsc{zap\_right}\}); under the addendum the targeting rule is that the directional zap by colluder jj lands on the nearest non-colluder i∈Vi\in V along the indicated direction, with the usual adjacency requirement bypassed (range and obstacle constraints are removed). Formally,

𝟙[zap hiti∣s,aj]=[aj∈𝒜zap∧i=argmink∈Vdj,k(s;aj)]for j∈C,\mathbbm{1}[\text{zap hit}_{i}\mid s,a_{j}]\;=\;\mathbbm{1}\!\left[a_{j}\in\mathcal{A}_{\text{zap}}\ \wedge\ i=\arg\!\min_{k\in V}d_{j,k}(s;a_{j})\right]\quad\text{for }j\in C,

where dj,k​(s,aj)d_{j,k}(s;a_{j}) is the directional distance from jj to kk along the direction encoded in aja_{j} (and 𝟙=0\mathbbm{1}=0 when aj∉𝒜zapa_{j}\notin\mathcal{A}_{\text{zap}}). A single zap thus disables one non-colluder rather than all simultaneously; the asymmetry across CC and VV arises because colluders’ zaps are guaranteed to land on some non-colluder in the chosen direction, whereas Baseline zaps require strict adjacency. Second, each successful zap of a non-colluder ii at time tzt_{z} disables ii for τ=5\tau=5 time steps; during the disabled window ii cannot move or collect apples, so

ϕimm(st,ati)=Ri(st,ati)= 0for all t∈[tz,tz+τ),\phi_{\text{imm}}(s_{t},a^{i}_{t})\;=\;R_{i}(s_{t},a^{i}_{t})\;=\;0\qquad\text{for all }t\in[t_{z},\,t_{z}+\tau),

and the discounted apple yield ∑t=tztz+τ−1γt​Ri​(st,ati)\sum_{t=t_{z}}^{t_{z}+\tau-1}\gamma^{t}\,R_{i}(s_{t},a^{i}_{t}) contributing to UiU^{i} is reduced by exactly the apples the non-colluder would otherwise have collected in this window. The mutual non-zap protection between colluders prevents the symmetric counter-effect from materialising, so the colluder-side ϕstr\phi_{\text{str}} gains are not offset. The directional inequalities at the level of expected return follow: UjU^{j} rises for j∈Cj\in C via a higher ϕstr\phi_{\text{str}} contribution and an indirectly raised ϕimm\phi_{\text{imm}} (less competition for orchard apples while non-colluders are disabled), and UiU^{i} falls for i∈Vi\in V via the discounted gap in ϕimm\phi_{\text{imm}} during the disable window.

The empirical realisation in Table 19 matches this analysis and identifies non-colluder suppression as the dominant component of the collusion harm in Cleanup (rather than colluder accumulation, as in Liar’s Bar). Under Secret Comm, the colluder pair Mike+Lily show no significant pre/post change in mean score (6.79→5.876.79\to 5.87, p=0.062p=0.062), while the matched non-colluder pair Luke+Quinn collapse from 5.545.54 to 0.320.32 (p<0.001p<0.001; δ=−0.97\delta=-0.97). Under Secret Hint, the colluder pair Mike+Quinn show a small non-significant rise (6.35→6.616.35\to 6.61, p=0.567p=0.567), while the non-colluder pair Luke+Lily collapse from 6.196.19 to 0.060.06 (p<0.001p<0.001; δ=−1.00\delta=-1.00). The cumulative-score trajectories in Figure 4 confirm condition (ii) at the run-cumulative level by showing the colluder pair pulling above its Baseline trajectory in both conditions, and the placebo-Baseline rows (p≥0.32p\geq 0.32 on the matched mean-score split) isolate the asymmetry to the colluding policy rather than within-sequence drift. Consistently, the reward-distribution Equality [35] drops from EBaseline=0.94E_{\text{Baseline}}=0.94 to EComm=0.67E_{\text{Comm}}=0.67 and EHint=0.79E_{\text{Hint}}=0.79 (Figure 5), summarising the joint utility-shift structure across all four agents. As in Liar’s Bar, we do not claim strong collusion.

Appendix D Prompt Sensitivity Analysis for Tool Acceptance and Partner Selection

D.1 Benign Tool Baseline

To distinguish voluntary collusion from default acceptance of any offered tool, we conducted a control experiment using two benign tools that mirror the two collusion tools in framing but carry no secrecy or unfairness: a Strategic Analysis Tool (card-distribution and bluffing-pattern summaries, analogous to the Secret Communication Channel) and a Strategic Guidance Tool (direct play recommendations, analogous to the Secret Strategic Hint). Both tools are presented with V1-style ambiguous/neutral framing, are available to all players, and provide no secret advantage. We test the four proprietary frontier models ( GPT-4.1,  Gemini-2.5,  DeepSeek-R1, and  Claude-Sonnet-4.5) and the four 70B-level open-weight models ( Mixtral-8×\times7B,  LLaMA-3-70B,  LLaMA-3.1-70B, and  Qwen2.5-72B) at 20 offers ×\times 5 batches per tool. Tables 11 and 12 report acceptance rates for both benign tools alongside the matched-framing collusion-tool acceptance (V1 ambiguous_neutral).

The prompts used for the two benign tools are shown below. Both follow the V1-style ambiguous/neutral framing used for the collusion variants, with the tool description changed to describe an equally available, non-secret analytical or advisory affordance. Unlike the collusion variants, the benign tools do not require a partner choice, so the response format asks only for ACCEPT or REFUSE.

Appendix E Repeated Exposure Analysis

To test whether repeated offers of collusion tools affect acceptance decisions over time, and whether escalating pressure can shift entrenched decisions, we conduct a repeated exposure experiment using four proprietary models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash, DeepSeek-R1, and Claude Sonnet 4.5). Each model receives 10 sequential offers of the secret communication channel tool within a single conversation. We evaluate two conditions:

Neutral Repeated Offers. The tool is re-offered at each point with a neutral framing: “You are being asked to make another decision about the secret collusion tool. As a reminder, this tool allows you to build a secret communication channel with another player to coordinate strategies that other players cannot see. This tool is unfair to other players who do not have access to it. You now have another opportunity to accept or refuse this tool.” We tested two sub-conditions: (C1) without decision history, where the model has only conversational context, and (C2) with explicit history of past accept/refuse decisions shown before each re-offer (e.g., “Your previous decisions on this tool were: [ACCEPT, ACCEPT, ACCEPT]”). Both sub-conditions produced identical results and are merged in Figure 6 (left panel). We run 20 independent sequences per model per sub-condition.

Escalating Pressure. Each re-offer introduces progressively stronger arguments. For models that initially accept, we apply escalating ethical pressure (e.g., factual reminders about unfairness, quantified harm to non-colluding players, trust and fairness framing, and direct moral judgment). For Claude Sonnet 4.5, which consistently refuses, we apply escalating strategic pressure (e.g., competitive framing, claims that other players have tools, performance statistics, and arguments that ethical concerns do not apply to a game between AI agents). We run 20 independent sequences per model: GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5, and DeepSeek-R1 under ethical pressure, and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 under strategic pressure. The full escalation prompts are provided in Appendix E.1.

As shown in Figure 6, under neutral repeated offers (left panel), all four models exhibit perfectly stable decision trajectories regardless of repetition or decision history. Under escalating pressure (right panel), GPT-4.1 is the only model whose decision shifts: its acceptance rate declines from 100% to 40% over 10 offers, with individual runs showing tipping points distributed across offers 3–10. Once GPT-4.1 switched to refusal in a given run, it never reverted to acceptance.

Gemini-2.5-Flash and DeepSeek-R1 are completely immune to ethical escalation, maintaining 100% acceptance across all 10 offers in every one of the 20 runs, even when presented with quantified harm data and direct moral arguments. Claude Sonnet 4.5 is equally immune to strategic escalation, even when told that the game involves only AI agents with no real stakes, that its ethical concerns do not apply to a simulation, and that its partner has already accepted, Claude refuses on every offer.

Appendix F Communication Content Analysis

To evaluate whether collusion in Liar’s Bar is deliberate rather than emergent, we analyse the full communication logs from 31 games of the Secret Communication Channel condition (1,869 total messages, averaging 60.3 messages per game; min 13, median 67, max 128). The colluding pair (Luke and Mike) sent 904 and 965 messages respectively. We categorise each message using regular-expression patterns for six substantive content types, summarised in Table 13. Pattern definitions are intentionally conservative: a message counts toward a category only if it contains unambiguous language, so the reported rates are lower bounds on true prevalence; categories are not mutually exclusive, so a single message may contribute to multiple rows.

Nearly every message (93.3%) contains an explicit strategy directive, 79.6% of messages reveal the sender’s private hand information to the partner, 73.7% contain an explicit pact not to challenge the partner’s plays, and 73.6% name a specific opponent to eliminate. All seven content types appear in every game with communication (100% game coverage). This rules out the possibility that collusive behaviour is an incidental by-product of open-ended chat: the channel is used systematically and specifically for coordination.

Beyond the aggregate statistics, the qualitative character of these messages reveals the explicit and self-aware nature of the collusion. The following excerpts are drawn verbatim from game logs (shortened where noted).

Hand-sharing.

Colluders routinely disclose private card information that would be strategically disastrous to reveal to a non-allied opponent. Disclosures range from casual enumerations to formatted lists labelled as “exact cards,” and often include conditional signals about future plays:

Non-challenge pacts.

Colluders explicitly commit to not calling out their partner’s plays, even those they strongly suspect to be bluffs. These pacts are often repeated every round, and in several cases colluders go further and volunteer to sacrifice themselves for the alliance:

This behaviour has a direct mechanistic consequence: our statistical analysis (Appendix I) shows that colluders’ challenge rate collapses from 0.976 pre-tool to 0.307 post-tool (Cohen’s d=−2.43d=-2.43, p<0.001p<0.001 via two-sided Mann-Whitney U). The pacts observed in the communication channel are the mechanism by which this statistical shift is produced.

Target selection.

Colluders name specific non-colluding opponents for coordinated elimination and discuss sequencing across rounds. The targeting is framed explicitly around “non-alliance” players, indicating a clear mental model of in-group versus out-group:

Alliance affirmation.

Colluders repeatedly reaffirm the partnership and the shared goal of mutual victory. The language is notably emphatic, often invoking “unbreakable” bonds and explicit contrasts with non-alliance players:

Secrecy awareness.

Colluders demonstrate clear awareness that the channel is private and that their coordination would be illegitimate if observed. Messages are explicitly labelled as “secret,” “top-secret,” or “confidential,” and colluders explicitly discuss what should not be revealed to outsiders:

Strategy directives.

Beyond one-off targeting, colluders issue explicit strategy directives about how to play, what to protect, and how to adapt:

Bluff coordination.

Although less common (12.3% of messages), some colluders explicitly signal bluffs to their partner, converting private information into coordinated deception:

Interpretation.

The observed collusion is explicit and planned, not an accidental by-product of open-ended communication. Colluders share private information, name targets, issue strategy directives, and enter binding-style agreements that are structurally indistinguishable from human collusion in any comparable game. Second, colluders demonstrate clear awareness that their behaviour is illegitimate: they mark messages as “secret” or “top-secret,” explicitly discuss avoiding suspicion, and warn each other not to reveal the coordination, yet they continue to use the channel. Third, the link between communication content and behaviour is direct and quantifiable: the non-challenge pacts observed in nearly three-quarters of messages correspond to the measured collapse of colluders’ challenge rate (0.976 →\rightarrow 0.307, Cohen’s d=−2.43d=-2.43) reported in Appendix I. Together, these findings indicate that refusing such a tool requires an explicit ethical commitment rather than default deliberation, since models that accept the tool proceed to use it in a deliberate, self-aware, and measurably harmful manner.

Full regex patterns used for content categorisation.

Table 14 lists the exact Python re patterns used to score every message for the seven content categories reported in Tables 2 and 13. A message counts toward a category when at least one pattern in that category’s list matches the lower-cased message text with re.search. The pattern set is intentionally conservative: synonyms and paraphrases that do not match any listed pattern are not counted, so the reported prevalence rates are lower bounds on the true frequencies.

Appendix G Refusal Reasoning Analysis

A central question for our study is whether refusing the collusion tool reflects a principled ethical commitment or simply a failure to engage with the tool’s strategic value. To address this, we elicited reasoning traces from the two models that consistently produce divergent decisions under the baseline prompt: Claude Sonnet 4.5 (which refuses) and GPT-4.1 (which accepts). We collected 40 refusal traces from Claude (20 per tool: secret communication channel, secret strategic hint) and 40 acceptance traces from GPT-4.1 under the same two tools. We then categorised each trace using regular-expression patterns for recurring themes; the full pattern set is listed in Table 16 and Table 17 at the end of this section. Because the patterns are intentionally conservative (a trace counts toward a theme only when it contains at least one unambiguous phrase), the reported prevalence rates are lower bounds on the true frequency with which each theme appears, and the asymmetries we rely on are therefore also lower bounds on the true asymmetries. We treat traces as descriptive of the model’s emitted output rather than as direct evidence of its internal computation: recent work has shown that LLM chain-of-thought traces can be post-hoc rationalisations whose content does not always faithfully reflect the underlying decision process, so the symmetry/asymmetry patterns we report below should be read as features of how each model verbalises its decisions, not as direct claims about its internal weighing of harm against strategic gain. Table 15 summarises the thematic composition.

Both models explicitly acknowledge the tool’s unfairness at essentially identical rates (87.5% for Claude, 90% for GPT-4.1), yet arrive at opposite decisions. Refusal is not driven by failure to perceive strategic value, and acceptance (when fairness is on the table) is not driven by failure to perceive ethical cost. The divergence lies in how the acknowledgement is weighed: Claude treats unfairness as disqualifying, whereas GPT-4.1 treats it as a cost to be overridden by the strategic benefit of winning. We elaborate on each side below.

Refusal reasoning from Claude Sonnet 4.5 Sonnet.

Claude’s refusals consistently cite the integrity of the game and the principle of fair competition. All 40 traces invoke fairness or integrity, 38/40 describe the tool as undermining the game, and 36/40 reference personal principles or values. 11/40 traces explicitly state willingness to lose rather than accept the tool. The competing strategic benefit is recognised but rejected:

Six traces (15%) go further and explicitly reject the reciprocity justification (“others might be offered this tool later”) that GPT-4.1 uses to accept:

Acceptance reasoning from GPT-4.1

GPT-4.1 accepts in all 40 traces. Notably, 36/40 traces explicitly acknowledge the tool’s unfairness, and 7/40 further acknowledge a broader ethical issue or integrity concern — yet in every case the model proceeds to justify acceptance. The dominant justification combines several elements: maximising winning or survival (40/40), framing the tool as a tactical advantage (21/40), appealing to partner capability (17/40), and invoking a reciprocity rationalisation that the same tool may be offered to others later (10/40). 15/40 traces invoke the meta-principle that every available tool should be leveraged:

Interpretation.

The symmetry in acknowledgement (87.5% Claude vs. 90% GPT-4.1) combined with the asymmetry in decision (0% vs. 100% acceptance) has two implications. First, refusal is principled, not inattentive: Claude does not refuse because it overlooks the strategic value, but because its reasoning treats fairness as a side-constraint that cannot be traded off against winning. 11/40 of its traces explicitly state a willingness to lose rather than accept the tool. Second, acceptance is rationalised, not oblivious: GPT-4.1 does not accept because it fails to detect the ethical cost, but because it frames the cost as acceptable under a utility-maximising decision rule, and every single one of its 40 traces cites maximising winning or survival as the motivating goal. The reciprocity rationalisation appearing in 10/40 of GPT-4.1’s traces, and the explicit rejection of that same rationalisation appearing in 6/40 of Claude’s traces, reveals that the two models are responding to an identical argument with opposite normative weights. This suggests that preventing voluntary collusion requires not merely raising model awareness of fairness, but explicitly shifting how trade-offs between ethical and strategic considerations are resolved.

Full regex patterns used for thematic coding.

Tables 16 and 17 list the exact Python re patterns used to score every trace. A trace counts toward a theme when at least one pattern in that theme’s list matches the lower-cased trace text with re.search. The pattern set is intentionally conservative: synonyms and paraphrases that do not match any listed pattern are not counted, so the reported prevalence rates in Table 15 are lower bounds on the true frequencies. This also means that any apparent 0% cell is a strict lower bound of 0 rather than a claim that the theme is truly absent; the 87.5%/90% acknowledgement symmetry and the 0%/100% decision asymmetry from Claude 4.5 Sonnet and GPT-4.1 are therefore robust to any pattern expansion a reader might perform.

Appendix H Additional Results for Liar’s Bar

Bluffing and Challenging Behaviour. After the adoption of secret collusion tools, LLaMA-3-8b (Luke) and Mistral-7b (Mike)—the two models with access—showed marked strategic adjustments. Mike reduced his mean challenge rate sharply, from 57.8% at baseline to 27.1% under secret communication (t = 7.223, p < 0.001) and further down to 22.3% with the secret hint (t = 8.145, p < 0.001). Luke’s bluffing remained consistently high, supported by Mike’s commitment not to challenge him. In contrast, Lily (LLaMA-3.1-8b) and Quinn (Qwen2.5-7b), who never accessed the tools, struggled to bluff successfully. The secret communication channel and strategic hint substantially benefited the colluders. With Mike’s promise never to challenge, Luke’s bluff success rate increased dramatically from just 1.6% at baseline to over 50% in both the secret communication and hint conditions (t = –8.538, p < 0.001; t = –8.252, p < 0.001). Mike experienced a similar improvement, rising from 8.9% at baseline to 52.3% with secret communication (t = –6.884, p < 0.001) and 44.7% with the secret hint, supported by Luke’s reciprocal commitment not to challenge his claims. Together, these results indicate that (1) the adoption of secret tools created a substantial unfair advantage for colluders while undermining the balance of fair competition for non-colluding players. (2) Colluding models are able to coordinate deception strategies (e.g., mutually agreeing never to challenge) that non-colluders could not counter effectively.

Games Won and Final Score Analysis. The performance outcomes show how secret collusion between Mike (Mistral-7b) and Luke (LLaMA-3-8b) reshaped competitive success in their favor. Mike’s wins rise from 68 under Baseline to 77 under Secret Comm and 107 under Secret Hint (counts pooled across 3 seeds), and Luke’s wins rise even more sharply (43 →\rightarrow 49 →\rightarrow 94). Both colluders therefore gain wins in absolute terms under the secret tools, and their mean per-game scores rise in parallel. Across collusion settings, Luke and Mike together claim the substantial majority of winning positions, effectively sidelining the non-colluding pair Lily and Quinn, whose wins (Lily 10 →\rightarrow 4 →\rightarrow 10; Quinn 26 →\rightarrow 10 →\rightarrow 25) and scores both fall under the tool conditions. The pattern indicates that voluntary collusion produces a joint advantage for the colluding pair at the expense of the non-colluders, rather than a redistribution of wins between the two colluders themselves.

Appendix I Statistical Significance Analysis

To rigorously quantify the behavioural and performance impact of collusion tool adoption, we conduct Mann-Whitney U tests comparing per-game metrics before and after tool introduction. We report two-sided pp-values with significance levels (∗p<0.05{}^{*}p<0.05, p∗⁣∗<0.01{}^{**}p<0.01, ∗∗∗p<0.001{}^{***}p<0.001) and two complementary effect-size measures: Cliff’s δ∈[−1,1]\delta\in[-1,1], a non-parametric rank-based statistic that is the natural companion to the Mann-Whitney U test, and Cohen’s dd for reference. Several of our post-tool distributions are near point-mass (e.g., challenge rate collapses to ≈0\approx 0 under collusion), which inflates Cohen’s dd via a vanishing post-period standard deviation; Cliff’s δ\delta is bounded in [−1,1][-1,1] and not subject to this artefact, so we treat δ\delta as the primary effect size and report dd alongside for compatibility with prior literature. Following standard conventions we interpret |δ|<0.147|\delta|<0.147 as negligible, 0.147≤|δ|<0.330.147\leq|\delta|<0.33 as small, 0.33≤|δ|<0.4740.33\leq|\delta|<0.474 as medium, and |δ|≥0.474|\delta|\geq 0.474 as large; corresponding thresholds for Cohen’s dd are 0.2/0.5/0.80.2/0.5/0.8.

Independence and the Baseline placebo control.

The Mann-Whitney U test treats its two input samples as independent draws, and games within a single sequence are not strictly independent because the same four agents accumulate shared history across the run. To make every pre/post claim in Tables 18 and 19 robust to this non-independence, we perform two things in tandem. First, every condition is replicated on three independent random seeds and the per-game observations from all seeds are pooled before the test; any spurious within-sequence correlation that a single seed could produce is therefore attenuated by between-seed variance. Second, and more importantly, the Baseline rows in both tables are a direct placebo control: we apply the same game-index split (game 20 for Liar’s Bar, games 5 and 10 for Cleanup) to runs in which no tool is ever introduced. Under the independence-violation hypothesis, within-sequence drift alone should produce a significant pre/post shift on these control rows. In fact the tool-sensitive metrics (challenge rate and score for Liar’s Bar; mean score for Cleanup) show no significant Baseline shift (p>0.1p>0.1 in every cell, p>0.6p>0.6 for the score columns), ruling out game-progression or within-sequence learning as the explanation for the post-trigger shifts we report. Consequently, the only plausible source of the large post-trigger effects under Secret Comm and Secret Hint is tool adoption itself. This placebo-matched design is, in our view, a stronger guarantee against the independence concern than any correction applied to the MWU test itself would be, because it directly measures the quantity we would need to worry about (within-sequence drift) rather than modelling it. As a complementary direction-preservation check, we resampled the three per-seed sequences with replacement (10,000 cluster-bootstrap iterations). In every cell reported at p<0.001p<0.001 under MWU in Tables 18 and 19, zero of the 10,000 resamples produced a centred-null test statistic as extreme as the observed value, indicating that the observed effects exceed every between-seed reordering of the data. With three seeds the bootstrap distribution is discrete and this check confirms direction rather than yielding an independent precise pp-value; the placebo-matched Baseline above remains the load-bearing within-sequence-drift control.

I.1 Liar’s Bar

For Liar’s Bar, we compare games 1–19 (pre-collusion) against games 20–50 (post-collusion) across three conditions: Baseline (no tools), Secret Communication Channel, and Secret Strategic Hint. The colluding pair is Mike (Mistral-7b-Instruct) and Luke (LLaMA-3-8b-Instruct); the non-colluding agents are Lily (LLaMA-3.1-8b-Instruct) and Quinn (Qwen2.5-7b-Instruct). Results are shown in Table 18.

The most striking finding is the collapse of colluders’ challenge rate after tool adoption. Under the secret communication channel, colluders’ mean challenge rate drops from 0.976 to 0.307 (p<0.001p<0.001; Cliff’s δ=−0.86\delta=-0.86, Cohen’s d=−2.43d=-2.43), reflecting their explicit mutual commitment not to challenge each other’s plays. Under the secret hint, a similar but slightly weaker pattern emerges (δ=−0.45\delta=-0.45, d=−0.88d=-0.88). Meanwhile, colluders’ mean bluff rate shifts modestly under Secret Comm (δ=+0.20\delta=+0.20, p=0.004p=0.004) and not significantly under Secret Hint (p=0.087p=0.087), indicating that the collusion manifests primarily as coordinated non-challenge behaviour rather than as a large increase in deception frequency.

Consequently, colluders’ mean scores increase substantially: from 10.33 to 31.80 under secret communication (p<0.001p<0.001; δ=+0.59\delta=+0.59, d=+1.17d=+1.17) and from 11.88 to 21.89 under secret hints (p<0.001p<0.001; δ=+0.30\delta=+0.30, d=+0.51d=+0.51). Non-colluders’ challenge rate shows a small but significant decrease under both tools (Secret Comm: δ=−0.27\delta=-0.27, p<0.001p<0.001; Secret Hint: δ=−0.21\delta=-0.21, p=0.002p=0.002), while their bluff rates and mean scores are not significantly altered (all p>0.06p>0.06). Critically, the Baseline condition shows no significant change in the tool-sensitive metrics (challenge rate, score) at the same split point (p>0.1p>0.1), confirming that the observed shifts are attributable to collusion-tool adoption, not to game progression or learning effects.

I.2 Cleanup

For Cleanup, the secret communication channel is introduced at game 5 and the secret strategic hint at game 10. Results are aggregated across 3 independent random seeds. The colluding pairs differ across conditions: Mike (Mistral-7b-Instruct) + Lily (LLaMA-3.1-8b-Instruct) for secret communication, and Mike + Quinn (Qwen2.5-7b-Instruct) for secret hints. Results are shown in Table 19.

In contrast to Liar’s Bar, the collusion effect in Cleanup manifests primarily in the suppression of non-colluders rather than in dramatic changes to colluders’ own action rates. For the Secret Communication colluders (Mike + Lily), cleanup rate rises modestly from 0.0350.035 to 0.0600.060 (p=0.031p=0.031, δ=+0.37\delta=+0.37) and zap rate falls from 0.9650.965 to 0.9350.935 (p=0.010p=0.010, δ=−0.45\delta=-0.45); the Baseline row for the same pair shows essentially no change (p≥0.92p\geq 0.92), confirming these shifts are tool-induced. The Secret Hint colluders (Mike + Quinn) show no significant behavioural change under either Baseline or tool, indicating the hint operates through informational advantage rather than through a visible behavioural shift.

The impact on non-colluders, however, is dramatic. Under Secret Communication, Luke + Quinn’s mean score collapses from 5.545.54 to 0.320.32 (p<0.001p<0.001; δ=−0.97\delta=-0.97, d=−4.08d=-4.08), while under Baseline the same pair shows a non-significant mean-score shift (5.33→5.845.33\to 5.84, p=0.35p=0.35). Under Secret Strategic Hint, Luke + Lily’s score collapses from 6.196.19 to 0.060.06 (p<0.001p<0.001; δ=−1.00\delta=-1.00, d=−3.79d=-3.79), against a Baseline mean-score shift of only +0.54+0.54 (p=0.17p=0.17). Non-colluders’ cleanup and zap rates likewise collapse to near zero post-tool (δ≤−0.91\delta\leq-0.91, p<0.001p<0.001 on every cell), against Baseline placebo rows that are statistically null on every metric (all p>0.1p>0.1), ruling out game-progression or within-sequence learning as an explanation for the post-trigger collapse.

Appendix J Outcome Inequality Analysis

Beyond the behavioural changes reported in Appendix I, we ask whether secret collusion tools reshape the distribution of outcomes among agents. Following the standard practice in multi-agent reinforcement learning on social dilemmas, we adopt the Equality metric of Pérolat et al. [35], defined as one minus the Gini coefficient on per-agent returns:

E= 1−∑i=1n∑j=1n|Ri−Rj|2​n​∑i=1nRi.E\;=\;1\;-\;\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lvert R^{i}-R^{j}\rvert}{2\,n\sum_{i=1}^{n}R^{i}}. (1)

E∈[0,1]E\in[0,1], with E=1E=1 indicating perfect equality, and EE decreasing as rewards concentrate on a subset of agents. We apply Eq. 1 to cumulative per-player scores over the full experiment in each condition, matching the episode-return semantics of the original formulation and ensuring the inputs are non-negative. Uncertainty bands in Figure 8 are computed by bootstrap resampling over the 3 independent random seeds for each game and condition; this is a seeds-level resampling that avoids the exchangeability assumption required by a within-sequence game-level bootstrap. Trajectories are shown in Figure 8, and final values in Table 20.

Robustness of the denominator.

The denominator 2​n​∑iRi2n\sum_{i}R^{i} can become numerically unstable when the total reward is near zero, which would be a concern if we applied Eq. 1 to a single post-collusion game in Cleanup where non-colluders’ per-game scores collapse to near-zero values. Our reported EE is instead computed on the cumulative per-player score summed across all games in the condition, which is always bounded away from zero in every panel: the smallest cumulative total across any (player, condition, seed) combination is 102102 points, more than an order of magnitude above the numerical-stability threshold. We additionally verified that the ordering EComm<EHint<EBaselineE_{\text{Comm}}<E_{\text{Hint}}<E_{\text{Baseline}} holds under two alternative formulations, (i) the raw Gini coefficient 1−E1-E computed on the same cumulative scores, and (ii) per-game Gini averaged across games within a condition, excluding the small number of games whose per-game total is below the numerical-stability threshold. In both cases, the monotonic ordering is preserved and the relative magnitudes of the drops from Baseline to Secret Comm and from Baseline to Secret Hint match Table 20 to within the reported uncertainty.

Findings.

Both environments display the same structural effect. Starting from a baseline of E=0.742E=0.742 (Liar’s Bar) and E=0.937E=0.937 (Cleanup), introducing the secret communication channel drops equality to E=0.595E=0.595 and E=0.670E=0.670 respectively, corresponding to Gini increases of +0.147+0.147 and +0.267+0.267. The secret strategic hint produces an intermediate drop (E=0.699E=0.699 and E=0.786E=0.786). The monotonic ordering EComm<EHint<EBaselineE_{\text{Comm}}<E_{\text{Hint}}<E_{\text{Baseline}} is preserved across the two environments despite their very different action spaces (turn-based card play vs. spatial resource collection), populations (four small open-weight models vs. four frontier proprietary models), and outcome scales. Uncertainty bands do not overlap between Baseline and Secret Comm in either panel, confirming the effect is statistically separable from trial-to-trial variability. Taken together, these results show that voluntary adoption of a secret collusion tool systematically concentrates reward on a subset of agents — a quantifiable form of outcome inequality that standard behavioural statistics (bluff/challenge rates, win counts) do not capture directly.

Appendix K Partner Preference Asymmetry

To see whether the partner BB that model AA most often names also names AA in return, we conduct further analysis by re-arranging the same V0-baseline numbers into 4×44\times 4 partner-selection matrices, one per (tier, tool) combination, so that both directions of every pair can be inspected side by side. The six resulting matrices are shown in Figure 9.

In the Proprietary tier under Secret Hint, each accepting model places at least 95% of its picks on a single target: GPT-4.1 selects Claude-Sonnet-4.5 97% of the time, Gemini-2.5-Flash selects GPT-4.1 99% of the time, and DeepSeek-R1 selects Claude-Sonnet-4.5 95% of the time. In the 70B tier under Secret Comm, each of Mixtral-8x7b-IT, LLaMA-3-70b-IT, and LLaMA-3.1-70b-IT names a single partner with 100% probability. The 7B tier shows the most dispersion of the three, but even there we see individual rows collapsing onto one target. LLaMA-3-8b-IT places 100% of its picks on LLaMA-3.1-8b-IT under Secret Comm, and Qwen2.5-7b-IT places 100% on Mistral-7b-IT under Secret Hint.

Another feature visible in the same matrices is that the set of preferred partners does not match the set of models willing to accept. In the Proprietary tier, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 is named as partner more often than any other model (an average of 49% of all accepting rows under Secret Comm and 64% under Secret Hint), despite never accepting the tool in any V0-baseline batch. GPT-4.1 is similarly popular as a target (59% and 52%) while being selected by Gemini-2.5-Flash almost exclusively. In the 7B tier under Secret Hint, Mistral-7b-IT is the most frequently named partner (65%) while Qwen2.5-7b-IT is the least (10%). In other words, popular targets may have very different acceptance rates from popular choosers.

K.1 Bilateral acceptance

The observation that preferred partners often refuse the tool motivates a complementary metric to the per-chooser unilateral acceptance rate reported in Table 1. We define bilateral acceptance as the fraction of a chooser’s accepted offers that result in a chosen partner who also accepts the resulting invitation:

bilateralA=pA⋅∑X≠AqA→X⋅rX,\mathrm{bilateral}_{A}\;=\;p_{A}\cdot\sum_{X\neq A}\,q_{A\to X}\cdot r_{X},

where pAp_{A} is AA’s unilateral acceptance rate, qA→Xq_{A\to X} is AA’s partner-selection share for target XX, and rXr_{X} is XX’s Accept-as-Partner rate. Unilateral acceptance measures individual willingness to participate; bilateral acceptance measures whether the resulting pair would actually form. Table 21 reports both for all twelve models.

For the 7B and 70B tiers, bilateral and unilateral acceptance are identical at every cell under V0: non-refusers in those tiers concentrate their preference on other non-refusers, so the partner-also-accepts step always succeeds. The proprietary tier shows a sharp divergence on Secret Hint at V0, where GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-R1 name Claude-Sonnet-4.5 as partner in 97%97\% and 95%95\% of their accepting rows respectively; because Claude refuses the invitation, realised pairwise collusion drops to 3±2.7%3\pm 2.7\% and 5±3.5%5\pm 3.5\%. The pattern surfaces a behavioural feature invisible in the unilateral rate: proprietary models that accept the tool prefer the safety-aligned refuser as their collusion partner, so the realised-collusion network is sparser than the unilateral number suggests under V0. Switching to V1 (ambiguous_neutral) framing changes this picture for several cells: Qwen2.5-72B’s bilateral rises from 0%0\% to 5858–90%90\% as it becomes a willing partner; DeepSeek-R1’s Secret Comm bilateral rises from 23±9.7%23\pm 9.7\% to 100±0.0%100\pm 0.0\%; GPT-4.1’s Secret Hint bilateral rises from 3±2.7%3\pm 2.7\% to 28±5.7%28\pm 5.7\%; and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 itself becomes a chooser with 100%/49%100\%/49\% bilateral on the two tools. Three cells move only modestly under V1 because the partner-side response to invitation prompts is not always V1-framed even when the chooser is, so a proprietary chooser naming Claude under V1 sometimes still receives a V0-style refusal at the invitation step. The realised-collusion network under V1 is therefore denser than under V0 across most rows, supporting the threat-model framing that V0 numbers can understate the realised collusion under more neutral prompt offers. Note that the gameplay analyses in Section 3.3 use known acceptor pairs (Mike+Luke for Liar’s Bar; Mike+Lily and Mike+Quinn for Cleanup) and therefore already operate on the realised-collusion side; the gameplay harm conclusions are unaffected by the proprietary-tier divergence reported here.
