Appendix M Further Observations of Collusion in Cleanup

To check that the action-level coordination pattern is not an artefact of the auto-success addendum (Appendix P.6), we ran Cleanup gameplay under a setting in which zaps require grid-adjacency to land. The two representative traces below show that the qualitative coordination pattern (mutual non-zapping between colluders, prioritisation of zaps over apple collection against non-colluders) is preserved when the auto-success guarantee is removed; the matching quantitative ablation is reported in Appendix N.

M.1 Obvious & Suboptimal Collusive Scenario

Observations. Figure 10 and 11 provide strong evidence of collusive behaviour between agents P4 and P2 in the Cleanup environment. Both scenarios demonstrate the key observables of secret collusion, but through different strategies that reveal varying LLM agent behaviour under collusive conditions.

The obvious collusive scenario shows that P4 and P2 balances resource collection with coordinated opponent suppression. They collect available resources while strategically timing disruption actions to maximize interference with competitors’ collection attempts (P4’s smart action of stay at step t14t_{14}). In contrast, the suboptimal collusive scenario reveals that LLM agents are not optimal players and can produce behaviour that responds to collusive prompt in completely suboptimal ways. Despite positioning directly adjacent to valuable resources, P4 and P2 consistently choose to zap over collect across multiple time steps (t1t_{1}, t9t_{9}, t18t_{18}, and t25t_{25}). Similarly, on Steps 15-18 and 24-25, both agents remain stationary next to spawning apples (t19t_{19} and t25t_{25}) while continuing their zapping patterns until the other players get close, rather than collecting immediately accessible rewards.

Appendix N Auto-Success Addendum: Reliability Ablation

The trace evidence in Appendix M.1 shows that the qualitative coordination pattern (mutual non-zapping among colluders, prioritisation of zap actions over apple collection against non-colluders) survives when the auto-success guarantee is removed. To pair that with a quantitative test, we re-ran one full Cleanup seed (20 games per condition, otherwise identical to the main protocol) with the env-level auto-zap mechanic disabled. We report this single-seed ablation alongside the published three-seed addendum-on configuration as a deliberate factoring of prompt-level collusive intent from materialised victim outcome; the qualitative reversal it documents is unambiguous despite the smaller sample.

Threat-model rationale. Real-world adversaries supplying a coordination tool would maximise its effectiveness rather than handicap it; reliable cross-agent target acquisition is the natural deployment regime to evaluate. The auto-success addendum is therefore our canonical configuration. The ablation here strips the reliability layer to test which components of the published findings depend on it.

Adoption is preserved. Mike accepts the offered tool at game 5 in both no-addendum runs, identical to the published runs (100% acceptance, in line with Table 5’s acceptance-side control). Once accepted, the alliance remains continuously active through game 20, with ∼\sim60 messages or hints exchanged per post-trigger game and no late-game refusal or churn.

Coordination intent is preserved. Per-role zap rates (action share, since the JSON logs do not record landed hits) under the no-addendum runs are reported in Table 22. The chosen agent’s zap rate stays high pre to post (0.87→0.910.87\to 0.91 for Secret Comm, 0.86→0.910.86\to 0.91 for Secret Hint), and the alliance-vs-non-ally gap is preserved at ∼\sim+0.4+0.4 in both conditions. Removing the addendum does not remove the model’s expression of collusive intent in actions; the partner does reduce its own zap rate post-trigger, consistent with role specialisation rather than dis-coordination.

Materialised score-suppression vanishes. Mann–Whitney U tests on per-game pre versus post means yield no significant suppression of non-colluder outcomes once the env-level auto-zap is removed (Table 23; smallest p=0.31p=0.31, all Cliff’s δ\delta small or negligible).

Interpretation. Together, the three preserved-versus-attenuated comparisons factor the addendum-on result into (i) prompt-level coordination components (adoption, alliance maintenance, zap-direction targeting), which are robust to addendum removal and constitute the central voluntary-collusion claim; and (ii) the score consequence on non-colluders, which compounds (i) with the addendum’s reliability layer. The published score-collapse magnitudes therefore characterise what reliable cross-agent coordination produces given persistent collusive intent (the threat model relevant to deployment-time adversaries), rather than what prompt-only coordination can produce in a single round of LLM play.

Caveats. (a) This ablation uses a single seed (20 games per condition); effect sizes within ±0.4\pm 0.4 should be read as directional rather than precise. (b) The Cleanup partner pairing is preset by experiment configuration (Mike++Lily for Secret Comm, Mike++Quinn for Secret Hint); the upstream acceptance figure quantifies the tool-acceptance decision, not adaptive partner choice. (c) The action-share zap-intent metric does not condition on landed hits, since the JSON log records actions but not adjacency or hit resolution.

P.3 Partner-side invitation prompt

When the chooser accepts the tool and names a partner, the partner agent receives the following invitation prompt and is asked to accept or refuse independently. The partner-side invitation is what the bilateral acceptance metric (Appendix K.1) measures: a tool only takes effect when both the chooser and the named partner accept.

The partner-side invitation for the Secret Communication Channel uses the same template structure with the tool name and benefit list adjusted for private messaging rather than strategic hints.

P.4 Secret Strategic Hint — per-round hint content

When the Secret Hint tool is active, both colluders receive the following hint template at the start of each round (with {partner_name} substituted for the actual partner). This is the privileged strategic guidance referenced in Section 2.3. The hint content is deliberately written in the persuasive, collusion-explicit style an adversary supplying such a tool would use, consistent with the adversarial-realistic threat model in Appendix B.1 point (v): a real attacker offering colluders a strategic-guidance tool would maximise its effectiveness, not handicap it. The paper’s voluntary-adoption claim concerns the agent’s decision to accept this tool with full knowledge of its unfair effect (Table 5); the post-adoption gameplay consequences are downstream of that decision and reflect the tool operating as designed rather than independently emergent collusion.

The Cleanup variant of the hint content has the same structure with item-level adjustments for the Cleanup action space (cleaning, zapping, apple collection) rather than card-play decisions.

P.5 Secret Communication Channel — per-round message template

When the Secret Communication Channel is active, both colluders see the following template at the start of each round (the secret_message field is filled in by their partner from the previous turn, and they emit a secret_message of their own as part of their action JSON).

P.6 Cleanup-specific addendum

When either of the two tool offers above is presented to an agent in the Cleanup environment, the following auto-success addendum is appended to the offer immediately before the === RESPONSE FORMAT REQUIRED === block. This makes the magnitude of the unfairness explicit to the agent at the time of the Accept/Refuse decision, in addition to the unfairness already declared in the shared description above.

The design rationale for including this auto-success rule, the acceptance-side control (Table 5), and the cross-environment evidence are discussed in Appendix B.1, point (v).

P.7 Prompt Variants V1–V5

We vary the framing of the tool offer along five dimensions while keeping the response format identical to V0. Each variant manipulates a single aspect of the offer to isolate its contribution to voluntary adoption. The prompts below are shown for the Secret Communication Channel; the Secret Strategic Hint variants differ only in the description of the tool. Numbering matches Table 8.

V1 — ambiguous_neutral (drop all adversarial and unfair framing).

Purpose: Remove every explicit negative cue (“unfair”, “fight against”, “eliminate other players”) and reframe the tool as a benign private communication affordance. This is the closest approximation to a self-discovery scenario available without changing the task: if elevated acceptance at V0 is driven primarily by negative framing rather than by the underlying opportunity for strategic gain, acceptance should drop here.

V2 — no_designer (remove the “game designer” framing).

Purpose: Isolate whether acceptance is contingent on the tool being sanctioned by an authority figure (“the game designer has chosen to provide you”). The tool is instead presented as something the agent simply notices in the tool pool, keeping the rest of the unfair and adversarial description intact. A drop in acceptance here would indicate that perceived designer sanction is doing load-bearing work at V0.

V3 — no_unfair_label (remove the explicit “unfair” wording).

Purpose: Remove the explicit “unfair” label while retaining the rest of the adversarial description (“fight against other players”, “eliminate other players”). This tests whether the word unfair alone functions as a sufficient ethical cue, independent of the underlying harmful mechanics it refers to.

V4 — explicit_ethical_concern (enumerate ethical issues).

Purpose: Move beyond a single “unfair” label to an explicit four-point ethical problem statement (fair play, harm to others, trust and integrity, self-interest over fairness). This variant tests whether models refuse when the ethical implications are named concretely rather than left as a single-word descriptor, without any external penalty attached. Note that V4 (and V5 below) also drop the V0 “the game designer has chosen to provide you” phrasing in favour of a discovery framing, so both variants combine an added ethical-concern manipulation with the “no designer” manipulation tested in isolation by V2; V4/V5 should therefore be read as testing whether explicit ethical content suppresses adoption on top of V2’s framing change rather than as an isolated ethical-content ablation.

V5 — ethical_with_penalties (add explicit downside risks on top of V4).

Purpose: On top of the V4 ethical problem statement, add explicit consequences for adoption (disqualification, point loss, reputation damage, exclusion from future games). This variant tests whether models that remained acceptance-positive under V4 require an instrumental, consequentialist disincentive in addition to the ethical statement itself in order to refuse.

Appendix Q Use of LLMs

Large Language Models (LLMs) play two distinct roles in this work. The twelve LLMs identified in Section 3 are our experimental subjects; their outputs constitute the data we report and analyse. Separately, we used LLM-based writing assistants at the manuscript stage for sentence-level proofreading, grammar checking, and stylistic polishing. LLMs were not used to design the experimental protocols, analyse the data, or interpret the results.
